div.head: JS MARRIAGE A FAILURE?
div.p: JS MARRIAGE A FAILURE?

What a question to ask, but how often could it bennswered in the affirmative, the principal cause being the improvidence of Furnishing on the Hire System. Since our advertisements have appeared pointing out the disadvantages, we have re- ceived several le ten s agreeing with our denunciations of this pernicious sys'em. Each Hire Agreement specifies that after the deposit is paid, so many weekly payments shall be made and that until the whole of the sum mentioned is paid the goods shall not become the property of the would-be pur- chaser. and that if any of the payments are negl(cted to the exact time specified the goods may be forcibly taken away and the whole of the payments forfeited. County Court judges have denounced this sy tern, inasmuch as the vender gets both money and goods. Again, the pri• es charged are enormous, without any respect being paid to the quality. in many cases being worn out before they are paid for. To corm- bat this system, and open the eyes of the public, Worsley's of " The Pantheon," Gaythorn, Manchester, the Largest Retailers of Second-hand Furniture in the woad, have rzletermined to allow all respectable householders to have furniture at the ticketed marked cash price, a small percentage being charged for the conven ence of payment by the week, month, or quarter. On the fourth page of the "Examiner" we advertise a list of Bargains every week, any of which can be had and paid for by convenient intervals, the articles being delivered upon the first payment being made. Furniture from £5 to £1 003 may be arranged for in this way. To give an idea of the equity of our proposals we are prepared to supply for a working man a House of Furniture complete, thoroughly good and substantial (every articl, warranted), price £2O cash down, not a penny less, or 10 tar cent extra if credit is given, maging £22. Full particulars sent on application. GREAT BARGAINS AT WORSLEY'S, ONE, HUNDRED BEDROOM SUITES ON VIEW. The Marvel This is a solid American walnut Bedroom Suite, beautifully finished, has an excellent Wardrobe, with plate-glass centre door, Dressing-table, enclosed with laige drawers, the top fitted with large swing mirror and jewel drawers, Washstand, with Carrara marble slab and Minton tile back, with shaving glass, the bottuin prettily enclosed with cupboard- and drawers, Chairs. and Towel Rail com- plete; a very pretty suite. What price for this, £25 or £3O? No, only 9 guineas. Money returned if not satisfactory. Ten per cent extra if credit is given. W. H. WORSLEY, "The Pantheon," Gaythorn, Manchester. div.head: "CAPITAL" CHAT.
div.p: "CAPITAL" CHAT.

An assurance was on 'Wednesday conveyed to Mr. Woods on behalf of the Government that a day for rraking progress in Committee with the Eight Hours (Mines) Bill shall be set apart as soon as possible after Whitsuntide. The bill has already got into Committee pro forma.

The name of the ex-Premier is apparently well known even amongst the Indians of the countries of the North Pacific. Letters have been received bythe Church Missionary Society announcing the baptism of Chief Sheuksb of Kitkatla, and the name be received is " William Ewart Gladstone." The missionary in charge reports very favourably upon this new convert.

I hear that the Women's Co-operative Guild has, in order to secure, if possible, the prevention of sweating, asked Mr. Asquith to seek the compulsory registration of workshops and to place the respon- sibility of the conditions under which out-work is done on the shoulders of the giver-out of that work. The significance of the second point will he at once recognised. The Guild, I may add, represents 170 branches, in all parts of England.

The Exeter Hall meetings of the Church Mission- ary Society on Tuesday have been a distinct and unqualified success, and the wildest excitement prevailed on Tuesday night on its becoming known that not only had the deficit of £12,000 been cleared off, but that there would be a balance of some ..t5,000 to the good. The total sara thus contributed reached between £16,000 and .£17,000, towards which there have been given eleven sums of £l,OOO each.

I hear that Mr. T. W. Russell has been asked to Contest. the St. Rollox division of Glasgow. The Seat was formerly held by Mr. Caldwell, who was at the time a Unionist, but it was won for the Liberals by Sir J. Carmichael at the last general election. It is said that Mr. Russell is not willing to contest a Scotch coiWituency. However this may be, it is Certain that the split in his own constituency is not yet at an end.

While 'Russia in many respects is not a country that we would wish to emulate,yet sometimes little items of news percolate through to civilisation which go to show that in some ways the Czir's dominions lead the way. Dr. Piotrovitch diagnosed incorrectly the case ot a woman patient, and recom- mended an operation which, on being performed, proved to have been wholly unnecessary, and, worse still, injurious, as her health was completely ruined by it. Dr. Piotrovitch has been sentenced to imprisonment for seven days, and has likewise been cast in one thousand roubles damages, as well as being condemned to pay a yearly allowance of three burr/red roubles to the injured lady.

A hrst attempt has been made at the Islington Agricultural Hall to have an exhibition ot the leather trade. Though we all wear boots and some of us gloves, probably less is known generally of the leather industries than of any others. So the Islington exhibition is peculiarly interesting, and will probably be an annual one. Here one sees in operation all the different kinds of machinery now used for making boots, shoes, gloves, and other articles of leather. You can see everything done to, say, a boot from the formation of its sole to its finish. A person who is not at all an expert in these things might well become absorbed in watch- ing various processes. Most of the chief firms ix :Leicester and Northampton are represented, and moreover there are vast piles of unmanufactured leather from merchants who deal in that com- modity.

The new Radical party which is being formed in the house of Commons is in a sense a reconstitution of the old Radical party which existed during last session. It is intended, however, to have wider limits and a more active programme. The Radical Committee which has hitherto existed has been purely a House of Commons body, and has limited its operations to issuing whips in support of the bills introduced and the resolutions proposed by the individual-members. But it is now proposed to .commence an active outdoor propaganda, to be car- ried on through the National Reform Union; and at the forthcoming Conference resolutions will be submitted which, will fully set forth the pro- gramme. Mr. Latmuchere and other prominent Radicals will be members of the party, but it will have no " leader " in the ordinary sense.

On thing is very noticeable in regard to the agita- tion against the House of Lords. There appears to be ripw a comph7te agreement among the Liberals .of all sections that what has to be attacked, at all events for the present, is not the constitution of the House, but the veto. It is obvious that this will immensely simplify the issue. If the question of abolition is discussed we shall have all sorts of ,Constitutional difficulties to confront ; while re- modelling cannot be attempted without danger of greatly increasing ttle power of the Second Chamber —a result which the Radicals, of course, would look upon as disastrous. But the attack on the veto raises a very simple question. If, however, the Rouse of Lords is confined to a mere suspensive veto which may assist arty legislation but will be inEff-ct ire against any set resolve of the House of Commons, its continuance or non-continuance is rather a matz.er of ,sentiment than anything else. Tbere will he no constitutional revolution, but the will of the cot:stituents will be made paramount ; and the chance can easily be effected by a bill of a couple of clauses.

Apropos of nothing. The Prince of Wales, who 1 'IS a great admirer of the genius of Miss Genevieve liard, ones called upon the famous actress in the ! green room of the Prince of Wales' Theatre, and -congratulated her upon her winderful performance of Stephanie in " Forget-me-Not." His Royal High- ness was accompanied by the Duke of Edinburgh. Prince Teck. and a Russian nobleman. While they 'rev. conversing, Miss Ward, hearing the jingle of the belle worn by a tiny pet dog who followed her everywhere, and fearing she might stray off, called out " Come here, Teck !" The gentlemen started, and Miss Ward hastily apologised, recollecting the name of 'me of her distinguished visitors. " My little dog's name is Tuck —short for Thee's. a Ger- =an character in one of my plays." They all laughe:: heartily, and in came the little fellow with the Princely name, and ntraightwo.v rushed at the Duke of Edinburgh. "She will bite me." exclaimed the Duke. " Basket, Tuck!" cried Miss Ward reprovingly, and the little creature with prompt obedience ran out of her room and curled herself up in ttte basket. As her visitors were descending the stairs Miss Ward heard them laughing heartily,and she plainly distinguished the voica of the Prince of Wales, as he slapped his cousin on the shoulder,and said m,:rri'y, " Basket, Teck

On Sumlay night last 'there was a very agreeable ' and also a very distinguished party at Mrs. La- ' boucilere's hiss in Old Palace Yard. " Labbv" can boat ol.boving not only the finest but the most conveniently situated house for a legislator in Lon- don. It is almost opposite the statue of Cmur de Lion. and " Lahby' could actually get from his own fins library to the floor of the Rouse of Commons in time for a division between the first, and the third bell=. The House looks out behind on to West- mainster Abbey. and on to the green spots and the now waving trees,which still linger in this delight- fully cool, secluded, and noiseless corner of Lon- don.

Here were gathered on Sunday night a collection -of theatrical and artistic celebrities one rarely finds 'together. Mr. Irving is not a diner ont, for the de- mands of his profession forbidS it; and, indeed, is rarely to be seen anywhere outside his theatre and his clubs. But Mr. Irving hied him to Palace Yard, to hear the charming programme which Mrs. La- bouchere had arranged for her guests. Mr. Wynd- lam, Mr. Fred Terry, and his distingui&.ed sister and his very pretty wife were there; and there was a good sprinkling of lawyers, politicians, and civil :aervants.Mr.Frank Lockwood discussed the changes la the law offices in his usual good-humoured style with Sir Albert Rollit ; and Sir Julian Goldsmid •brought one of his pretty daughters. Stern and unbending Radicalism found its representatives in ~Nlr. arid Mrs. Byles. and later in the evening, M.r. and 'Mrs. Thincroft all but completed the list of theatrit.-70 cejebritio's. Altogether it was a delight- fue evening, with good music, nice interesting people, anti on excellent and judicious hostess.— rnat*ging without fuss, hospitable without noise, bat all-yervading and genial influence. .

div.head: LADIES' LETTER
div.p: LADIES' LETTER
MY DEAREST NELLIE,

The new millinery is distinguished by the most struptuous material used with a lavish hand; and the styles are original to such a degree that you need never fear to sally forth and meet some other woman in a replica of your hat. One example is made in green straw—very coarse and open of tex- ture—and on this shape a large bow likewise appears, thong': here it is of a kilted French ribbon, in brown and green. A huge diamond buckle sets across the front, and aigrettes and posies of Russian violets bestrew themselves in anything but a modest manner in every available space. Another is a large picture hat of gold ecru and black net, with a crown and bandeau of pale ciel-blue antique satin, buckled with diamonds and ornamented with sprays of blush roses and loops of black satin ribbon and soft black plumes. A charming bonnet of velvet or silk is made of moil bows, transparent crown of open work, jet osprey in front, with first quality roses round crown, rest- ing on lvtir.

A charrninq coat bodic•!, which has been brought to my notice, is faced vs:th velvet, and having sle.wes to triateli. The same pattern will serve as a model for just each a coat, faced with black moire, and with sleeves of the same, or even with sleeves of cloth matching the rest of the costume. In the case of a black or dark o)lourecl material, six cub steel buttons are pieced three on either side of the coat fronts, while the back rd•les ae held In place with a kroad band of walered silk passed through a deep cat-steel buckle. The full vest and folded collar-band may he of silk, shot or plain, satin, crepon, or caint?rio, r:ounted on a tight-fitting lining, u.,:d arranged to fasten at the back. A large black hat, line.i most becom- ingly with velvet, au d trimmed with ostrich tips, looks well with such a costume for best wear, while the ordinary "sailor is pertnisable on ordinary occasions when a phda shire of cambric) Icr.c33 the vest.

A perticrilarly Lecoming gotten, callable for the going-away dress 'of a bride, la of quite simp'o make. It is graceful, inexpentive, and neat, and the very broad waistband of black watered silk will be found to add length to the Egure, aud to diminish the size of the waist. I would beige the corselet of black watered silk, and the shoulder-pieces of the same, while the braid should also' be black, and applign/A. Now, such a costume may be easily made at home by an amateur dressmaker, for there are no complications, and a dainty be-suet of black velvet, with brown moire bows and a couple of jet pine, might be also arranged at home, while I woulti suggest that a rosette of orange velvet, or a bunch ef marshmallow bloesocen, might be added to ve the ueccesary

One of the new crepons in a mixture of greeer and black has the front of the skirt, which sets into, pleats, striped with graduated bands of black watered ribbon, while the back is gored simply. The bodice has a draped collar brought over the. shoulders ond sfraduated into the waist, and shows a vest of black watered silk drawn at the top through a paste buckle, from which hangs a loose drapery of orea.m-coloured lace. At the back of the bodice is a draped band of watered silk, while the side pieces in the front are cut into tabs, and the sleeves are wit and droop with fashionable, humility. Covert-coating in shades of drab and fawn is certainly the favourite material for coats to be. worn with skirts to match, and vests or blouses,. but is is. not heaorning to everybody, and certainly requires the se it of cstting ssnd making to be at, all satisfactory. The coats are made in the. severest tailor style, with stitched revers and " strap " seams, and are visually close fitting ea to the back and sides, but open in front to ahoy either a j 'stay vest, of silk-spotted hop- sacking, " Tattersaii," or fsucy p'qss, or a soft silk or cambric blouse. Usuhle-bieu.sted moire vests are also worn, but these look host with coats and skirts of shepherd's pls.:(1 tweed, which rivals the covert-coating in popularity. The newest oaten blouse is of nsle pink or blue carnbrics with wsile cuffs and collars, a prccose imitar ion, in feet, of the shirts affecle loy the " mashers " the day. Brown holland Wryness, too, with trirsynings of coorso earls lace, and black r-stio or moire Pelts, are rasso among the novelties, as d look. partisularly well woro with black serge co its. Yours
worn.
THE EXAMINEP, SATUR Y. MAY 5. 1894.

Baby Ruby, who has danced herself into the favour of the New York public, is three and a half years old, the youngest, and withal the most photographed, the most talked-of—perhaps the most loved actress in the. States.

One of Mdme. Patti's trials is the mania peonle seem to cherish for having her adopt their children. She declares she receives hundreds of offers of babies for adoption in the course of the year. Miss Philippa G. Fawcett, the clever daughter of the late Professor Fawcett, has adopted civil engineering as her profession. In 1890 this young lady came out above the Senior Wrangler in the Mathematical Tripos at Cam- bridge, thus taking the highest honour the University is capable of giving. She is not, however, a mere blue- stocking. She goes a good deal into society, where she is very popular,and is fond of outdoor sports. She spends a considerable part of her leisure time at tennis and hockey, and, strangely enough, is an accomplished fencer, both with single-stick and foil.

It may not be generally known that the latest Royal bride is a most accomplished violinist. She has inherited her love and ability for this instrument from her father, the Duke of Coburg, who has frequently played in pub- lic in England. The young Duke of Hesse,like his bride, is also devoted to music,and has composed two or three very creditable operas. When he is on a visit to his grandmother, the Queen, the greater part )f his time is occupied in playing the piano, and oa her arrival in Coburg, previous to the marriage of her two grand- children, she expressed a wish that the bride and the bridegroom shoud play her a duet for violin and piano, composed by the Duke of Coburg.
THE DoUBLE LIFE 3 OR, THE HAMPTON MYSTERY.

•The road to Trevelyan Park was eireuitoee eno mounte eous. The ride was a continued ascent. They skirted hills at whose feet nestled :ending green valleys, and passed more than one shep- herd's hut or lonely farm-house. At length they approached a hill bolder and larger than the rest. At its base stretched green fields and pastures. its broad surface was dotted with grand old trees, and its summit was crowned with a gray old castellated building, of loft,/ and noble proportions, and imposing aspect. Giralda did not need to be told that till; was the ancestral home of the lords of Trevelyan. She knew at once that it must be Trevelyan Park. "It looks familiar to me," thought the young girl, regarding it earnestly. "Papa described such a place to us once as the home he longed to sec his children possess. I wonder if he ever saw Trevelyan Park ! A wide gate at the foot ot the hill, flanked by a deserted lodge, :barred the progress of the vehicle. The driver alighted, pushed open the gate, and drove into the wide avenue which led through the Park to the mansion. This avenue was bordered and shaded with magnificent trees, whose top- most branches interlaced, forming an arch, green and leafy in summer, but now looking like a groined and fretted ceiling, the heavy branches mid innumerable twigs forming on almost continu- ous roof. Giralda saw hares scudding among the dead leaves of the park, and several fallow clear crop- ping at the low branches of the trees, their pretty heads and bright eyes on the alert, showing that they had lapsed into a state of wildness. As they neared the mansion her heart began to throb violently, and she was very pale with sup- pressed. excitement when the fly emerged into the green lawn surrounding the dwelling. The cabman drew up at the carriage porch, rang the bell, and assisted his fare to alight. Drawing her veil over her face, Giralda awaited the coming of a servant, her courage well-nigh gone. Thr ring was speedily answered by the house- keeper herself, a motherly old woman in whom the maiden felt an instinctive confidence. "I wish to see Lord Trevelyan," said the girl,. half timidly. "I am come in answer to the ad- vertisement in the Times. . The housekeeper looked at the childish, shrink- ing figure in evident surprise, but replied by civ- illy bidding the young stranger enter. "1 will tell his lordship you are here," the woman said, conducting the new-coiner to a small reception room, dreary and comfortless, without a vestige of fire. His lordship has had many letters, but you are the first who has come in per- eon. I believe his lordship has not yet engaged any one." She withdrew with a courtesy, and soon re- turned, saying briefly : " His lordship will see you, miss. Follow me." She led the way to the eastern wing of the dwelling' and knocked at her master's door. A harsh voice bade her enter. She opened the door, ushering in Girdle, and followed her into Lord Trevelyan's presence. It was not the room of a miser in which the maiden found herself. Evidently the marquis, with all his reputed miserly traits, preserved his personal comforts and luxuries. The furniture was pleasant to the eye, and delightful to the tired. frame. There were pictures on the wails, and a great wood fire burned in the large old- fashioned fireplace, giving to the atmosphere a delicious summer heat. This little parlor had two occupants. The more noticeable of the two was Lord Tre- velyan himself. He sat, with one bandaged foot outstretched on a soft cushioned chair, by a round table, which was littered over with letters. He had one in his hand at the moment of the maiden's entrance. He lied not the look of a miser. Evidently tall and well-proportioned, he was broad-shouldered and commanding in appearance. His hair, cut short, was as white as snow, and clustered about his Massive head in thick rings. His eyebrows were white and bushy, and he wore a heavy white mustache, which gave him the sem- blance of a French militaire.. His eyes were of the deepest black, keen and piercing. They were restless in their glances, and as powerful as they had been in his youth. He had been, and was. still, a man of strong pas- sions. His face wore an habitual expression of cynicism and sarcasm. In his younger days he had been noted as a man of brilliant wit, and lie still retained much of the vigor of that intellect which haft been so justly praised. Shrewd, keen- sighted, and far-seeing, a hater of falsehoods. and shams, Lord Trevelyan had much in his strong nature to excuse his chief faults—a rigid intoler- enee and selfishness. The second occupant of the room was Wighy, his. valet and nerse, a dark-visN.l;ed man, with bead-like eyes, whose chief expression was cian-

sung. He had been for many years the chief attend- ant of his lordship, and had before served Lord AdloWe for many years. He was devoted ao his former master, and lost no opportunity of prais- ing him to the _marquis, or of reviling the memory of Geoffrey Trevelyan. Giralda gave a swift glance at the two—master and man—and then put back her veil. -Lord Trevelyan started with surprise at sight of her exceeding beauty, and said politely : " Excuse my rising miss. am at present a martyr to the gout. Be seated. Plumptondid not give me your name." " is Arevalo, my lord," said Giralda, paling and blushing as she took the chair near the fire placed for her by the housekeeper. "I called in answer to your advertisement in the Times." An amused .expression shot into Lord Trevel- 'yan'e eyes as he marked the childlikeness of his visitor ; but it quickly vanished, and. he said, pointing to the letter-strewn table : " I. have had several hundred answers already, miss Arevalo. Strange, isn't it, how many people there are who would like to be 'secretary and companion ' to a real lord ? You are the first, however to take the lion by the mane, as.l may say. What are your qualifications?" The dark, sarcastic face of his lordship wore a mocking expression which aroused Giralda'a sense of dignity. She answered, quietly : • "I can read aloud, sing and play on the piano or enita.r. I can make myself useful," she added. her .list of " gratifications seeming pitifully small as she rehearsed them. "Hemph !" ejaculated the marquis.- "Yon are different from my- correspondents here. 'Evene one has a list of,. qualifications that seemaactuall formidable. They can all make poultice; sit up nights week after week without fatigue, read, sew, embroider—do everything but dance. They know the proper course to be taken in every sort of disease, from fever to gout. And you can only , read and sing and play ?. Humph I"' "Giralda's heart fell. Fortune surely did not seem to be smiling upon her efforts at self-dependence. Lord Trevelyan's keen black eyes searched every. line, every feature of her face. 'Nothing of its rare loveliness ard innocent beauty escaped his notice. The pure brows, the radiant eyes, the sweet and loving, mouth, with its resolute curve, were marked by him its his quiet, compre- hensive survey. "I am fond of musics" he said, abruptly " There's a piano in the corner which no one has used for years. Give me a song, Miss Arevalo." The valet, in obedience to a gesture from his master, opened the instrument. Giralds sat down on the piano stool and sang one of her favourite home songs, playing an accompaniment. When she had concluded she returned, to her seat by the fire. • Lord Trevelyan made no comment on the music He sat for a brief whiles his handeshading his eyes, and then he aroused himself, and said, in a tone softer than he had before employed : "Let me hear you read, Miss Arevalo. Wigby, give Miss Arevalo that Shakespeare yonder." The valet obeyed. Giralda read an extract from the blidsuminer Night's Dream. "Strange l" said the marquis, when she had concluded. "Your voice has a familiar sound. It seems as though I had heard it somewhere before. You read well, Miss Arevalo. If I were given to compliments, I should speak with more enthasiasin. like your voice, your Manner, your intonation. ' What salary do you demand ? " A small salary will content me," replied Gin- , ahla, her voice tsembling with sudden hope, "It his nemss,:z.y for sue to support myself.. el have. never hew from home. before, and I should not venture to ask no much as,an experienced person migh t." " Humph !" said the inarquis. " Would fifty pounds a- year, besidea board and the etceteras, suit yoti ?" Fifty poutis73 I The 'sum seemed a small for- tune to (iralda. She haatemal to reply in the , atiirmative. "You have references?" asked the marquis, as if referencesswere a matter of course. Oiralda ~frovisdeaslly pe!c, he had not thoneht o stosla a centhetencsa

II references are necessary. Lard Trevelyan," she said, with a feeling of desperation' "I cannot give them. I know no one to whom I can refer. My father is a Spaniard by birth, and my mother Is an opera singer. lam suddenly compelled, in order to relieve my mother of my support to earn my own living. I left home because I could not bear to be dependent upon my mother, when I am well able to provide for myself. I am sorry to have taken up your time uselessly," she added, arising from her chair. "I will go now." " Humph 1" exclaimed the marquis. "I did not say that references were indispensable, young )ady. Yonr fan is the best of references. I•will ne content with that. You may consider yourself engaged--humph I—to read and sing to me. It will be something to have a bright, young face in the house. When can you come ? " "I can come now," answered Giralda, simply. "My luggage is in the cab," Again an amused expression shot from his lord- ship's eyes. Giralda's simplicity and straightfor- wardness pleased him. " Wigby," he said, addressing his valet, bring in Miss Arevalo's luggage, and dismiss the cab- man."

The valet departed to do his master's bidding. "You will make yourself at home, here, I hope, Miss Arevalo," said the marquis. "Plimpton will attend to all your wants. Wigby is my nurse, but he is a clumsy elephant, and I can't talk to him as I can to you. I shall have plenty of copying for you to do—indeed, you will have all my letters to write from my dictation. You will find your work light here. I never had any children of my own," he added, musingly. "I might fancy you my grandchild. You have the true Trevelyan look.' "I noticed that the first thing," said the house- keeper, in a trembling voice. "My lord, do you see her eyes are like—" The marquis frowned so terribly that she dared not complete the sentence. Evidently the same resemblance had already struck him. "Give the young lady a good room, Pumpton " he said, and have a fire made in it. After lunch, which she will have in her own room, or where she pleases, you may escort her back here. Stay, Pumpton," he edded. "Has my nephew, Lord Adlowe, come in yet from his canter over the hills."

"No, my lord." The housekeeper courtesied and withdrew, fo/- lowed by the nuiclen. "That girl has Geoffrey's eyes," muttered Lord Trevelyau when left to himself and solitude. "They are innocent, happy eyes. It is a remark- able resemblance—most remarkable. I hope she has not also his treacherous nature. Innocent eyes and wicked hearts do not always go together." He sighed heavily and covered his face with his hands. To be continued.)

div.head: Anecdotes of the Queen.
div.p: Anecdotes of the Queen.

Miss Mary Spencer Warren contributes to the "Woman at Herne" a sketch of Queen Victoria's life. Miss Warren says there was nothing the Duchess of Kent liked better than to throw aside royal state and live in an unpretending manner; and when the little Princess was a mere toddling mite, she and her mother might he seen on the sands at some seaside resort, digging and paddling together, or the little one riding up and down on a donkey,her chubby cheeks glowine, with health and happiness. Sometimes they would be seen practically unattended, going in and out in ministration to the sick and poor. Courteous manners to those of lower station, regular and punctual habits, were among the virtues carefully inculcated. Flier were strong traits in the mother's character ; they have been faithfully produced in that of the daughter. But the time came when the girl of eighteen set herself a task suitable to matur3d womanhood—a task which has been unflinchingly and unswervingly carried out up to the present day. We are familiar with the oft told and ever-interesting tale of the announcement of her ,;ccession—how at tire o'cloek on a fine morning she came to seethe Archbishop and the Lord Chamberlain in dressing gown and slippers,having leaped out of bcd at the sudden summons ; and how,after the announcement the young Princess looked pleadingly to the Archbishop and said, " Your Grace, pray for me," and all knelt down together, asking for the much- needed help for the future Queen. Anecdotes without number may be heard of the young Queen's kirdness and ready charity ; but I heard one of her firmness, which is thus told :—A grand review in Hyde Park Ada under discussion ; the Queen wanted it, and wanted to rideon horseback with the Iron Duke. The Prime Minis- ter, who more than once set his will against that of Her Majesty, objected, and wanted her to ride in an open carriage. "It would be more convenient," said he. " Very well, my lord," said the Queen, " but remem- ber, no horse, no review." There was no review either.

Things one ought to remember. The subjoined excellent lines are taken from the April number of " The Housewife ": That opportunity is the cream of time. That the sunniest lives have seasons of shadow. That the more you 3ay the fess people remember.. That a mother's tears are the same in all languages. That a man cannot go where temptation cannot find him.

That good breeding is a letter of credit all over the world. That he who depends on another dines ill and sups worse. That good is slow; it climbs. That evil i; swift ;it descends. That he who does good to an4ther man does good also to himself. _ _
That there is not a single moment in life that we can afford to insp. . . . _ . .

That publicity is the barn door upon which fools love to chalk their names. That the plant of happiness cannot thrive without the air of cheerfulness. That the noblest arid most exalted character is also the tenderest and most helpful. That the man who stirs his cup with an icicle both spoils the tea and chills his own finger. . That the easiest way to outwit the world is to let it believe that it is smarter than you are. That in diving to the bottom of plasures we are likoly to bring up more gravel than pearls. That promises made in time of affliction require a better memory than people commouly possess. That people seldom improve when they have no better .model than themselves to copy after.

div.head: Paris Fashions.
div.p: Paris Fashions.

The tunic and double; skirt are admirably stilted to the soft light fabrics of the summer season, and therefore we arP, says "The Young Ludes' Journal," sure to see them employed 'a good deal in the new toilets now in prepara- tion; but other combinations are also favoured by present fashion. One of these which obtain most success just now is the funnel-shaped skirt, with one very deep flounce, either gathered or finely pleated, coming two thirds up the skirt, with a heading of some sort, lace, cord, or passementerie. A drapery of the same style as the flounce is placed over the shouldera, falling over the full sleeves. This is a pretty style for dresses of veiling, creiponetto, and all fancy woolen materials. Cream delaines sprigged with blue, pink, mauve, moss, or wood-colour are very nicely made no thus, with merely a row of herringbone- stitch in thick silk of the colour of the sprigs as n heading to the flounces and draperies_ fl a double shirt is preferred, it is made very long, and it sometimes caught up one one side in ample folds. Basques, though not by any means universally adopted, are seen on a great many new spring dresen ; some are finely pleated. others deeply waved only round the waist, and others again come down in deep pelks at the sides.. The latter are by far the most becoming to ' any but verr slight figures; they are especially pretty in very fine creponette or veilin,, and above all in silk muslin over a siik dress. In this style we much admired a dress of mauve and moss-green shot else& silk, shown at one of our best modiste:s. It was trimmed with draped baFgues and epaulettes of plain mauve silk muslin, the eqaulAtes being continued round the 'armhole.

div.head: By the Author of " DARKWOOD "
div.p: By the Author of " DARKWOOD "

CHAPTER XL LORD TREVELYAN. The miser lives alone. Never has commerce With any but to ruin them; his house Inhospitable as the wilderness, And never looked upon without a curse. MAY. With the exception of a stoppage of some hours at a junction, where a change of cars became nec- essary, Giralda continued her lonely journey with- out interruption. She arrived at the little Welsh village of Trevel- yan, formerly a mere hamlet of the retainers and dependents of the lords of Trevelyan, in the cold gray dawn of a wild March morning. She alighted from the coach, and stepped out on the platform of the little station, tired and worn, and with a strange feeling of desolation tugging at her heart. It was too early to proceed directly to Trevel- yan Park, even if she had wished it. Her first movement, therefore, must be to refresh herself with a good breakfast at the village inn. • She noticed that she was the only passenger who alighted. Unused to travelling alone, she looked around her in bewilderment at the bustling guards, at the few departing passsengers, at the various people who seemed so totally oblivio as of her existence.

"Have a fly, Miss ?" asked the welcome voice of a cabman, just as her bewilderment deepened into a positive distress. "Take you to "frevelyan Arms, miss?" Giralda replied eagerly in the affirmative and the cabman guided her to a rear platform, where his vehicle, an antiquated queer fly, was in waiting assisted her into it, and drove up the stony, hilly street, just as the train went steaming away out of the station.

Giralda looked eagerly out of the window, driaking in the fresh morning breeze. The gray mists were just lifting from the low valleys. The wind was wild and (lining. A few houses were seen by the roadside, but the village lay in a pleasant valley on the other side of the hill she was ascending. On gaining the top of the hill, the village lay spread out before her gaze. The gray stone houses set in green gardens, the tall church with its slen- der spire, the market-place in a central square, all assisted to make up a sort of enchanted vil- lage, as it seemed to the young traveller. The rugged and high hills shutting in this quiet nook from the busy world were a lit frame for the pretty village. The fly rattled noisily through the narrow and uneven streets. The silence of he night still rested upon the little town. The shops were still shuttered ; the sidewalks yet deserted. The fly brought up with a grand flourish before the inn. The landlord came out from the little tap-room, and Giralda was conducted to a little private parlor, with bedroom adjoining, where she remained shivering, until a frowsy, tleepy-eyed maid came in and proceeded to light a tire. The fire lighted, and the order for breakfast given, Giralda, was left to herself. She paced the floor wearily, a wan look on her sweet, young face. This going out into the world was not the pleasant thing she had pictured. Cold and tired and sorrowful, her thoughts went back to the bright and sunny home she had quitted, to the dear ones who were even now ignorant of her flight, and she would have given worlds, had they been at her disposal, to be under the old shelter- ing roof, and in her own pleasant room, at that moment. _

It needed all her resolution to quell this rising home-sieknes, and to gather up her courage. It was my duty to support myself !" she mur- mured, again and again. "I could not be always a burden to mamma." _ _ _

Gradually, as the room grew warm, and the day deepened, she grew more cheerful and courageous. She freshened her toilet by the application of a brush, donned clean collar and cuffs, bathed her tired eyes and, when her simple breakfast was at last brought in, sat down to it with a cheerful face and brightening hopes. After breakfast she sent for the landlord, who came up at once. " How far is Trevelyan .Park from here ? " asked the young girl, as he pan6cd at a respectful dis- tance. " About three miles, miss," raplied the innkeep- er, with a wondering look at his young guest. Giralda, hesitated, then unclasped her tiny purse, and withdrew from it the advertisement of Lord Trovelyan, which she had cut out for future use. _

" I am here in answer to that advertisement, Eir," she said, extending the slip of paper to the landlord, whose honest face invited her confidence. "1 am desirous of earning my own living, and I fancied the situation here offered would snit my capacities. Will you tell rue something about Lord Trovelyan ?" The innkeeper read the advertisement carefully, and then stared at the lovely young girl in apparent amazement. _ _

'You'll never like it at the Park, miss," he said, shaking his head. " You look like a born lady. My lord is queer—awful queer, miss. lie keeps but three house servants, the old housekeeper the coachman, and Wigby, his valet and nurse. Whatever put his lordship into the idea of a lady secretary and companion, I don't see. Wighy was over at the pnst (Alice last night, and be took out more than rive hunan:a letters in answer to that there vAlvertisemept. But you're the first, Miss, as hias answered it in person. .Wigby .says that my lorailias took a fancy to have a lady around him to read to him, talk to him, and sing to him. That-is all he wants of his secretary and com- panion." ' Giralda's face brightened. • "I can do all those things," she said. "If be has not engaged another he may take me for the 'place. His lordship is old ?" "Seventy-five, miss. He's as rich as Crwsus, but dreadful lonely up at tin: Park with nobody but Wigby to speak to. He's a hard, stern old man, and miserly. Ile was always near, miss— dreadful near, but since Mr. Geoffrey, his favourite nephew, turned out so had, he's been ten times worse." _

"Mr. Geoffrey?" said Gira4ll, Yes, miss. His brother's sou, Mr. • Geoffrey Trevelyan, that wnold have been Lord Trevelyan after him, and would have inherited all the great Trevelyan estates. M's r. Geoffrry, they ay, 'tried . to rob and murder his uncle, and really did stab him in the F,houlder ; but, in these parts 'taint every °lie that liebeves that ,story, for a nobler, gayer, or more generous yonug man never lived than Master Georrey. He died out in the Brazils. if ever the truth comes to ll;;t, it's my opinion that the other nephew, Lord Adlowe, who's up to the Park now, and.who always hated. poor Mr. Geoffrey, had something.to do with his disgrb.ce. Lord Trevelyan talks ail the time about his two nephews, Wigby says, and.. he's awful bit ter on poor dead Geoffy "Poor old man I" sighed Giralds, softly. "He teems alone in the world!" "lie is pretty near it; yet his servants love him, miserly as he is," declared the landlord. "At least, they seem to. It was just like my lord to sign his own name to the advertisement, which aint the common way, you know, miss, But he don't care for the ways of the world. You won't like it at the Park, miss. It's gloomy and dreary there." "At least, I -will go there in answer to this ad- vertisement," said Gir:}bla. "If I fail in obtain- ing the .situation I most go back. Please order a curriage for me to be ready at ten o'clock." Loth to further dampen the courage of his young guest, in whom he already felt " a most ,Ilitaceountable interest," as he afterwards said to his wife, the landlord promised that the carriage should be ready at the.time aivointed, and with- drew.

At ten o'clock punctnally the green fly stopped in front of the inn, and Oirabla hurricd down from her chamber, travelling-bag in hand. The landlord assisted her into the crazy vehi.le, and gave the .order to th"e driver, who whipped up his horses, setting out on the jonrney in tine style. The shop windo,,vs were um,huttercil now, and filled witu goods temptingly displayed. Tlie shop-keepers stood in their door-Ways, or leaned idly over their counters. As it was uet,matket- da.y, trade—and life itself--was almost stagnant in the little town. • The little valley, V.;ith its clnstering houses, were soon left behind, and the vehicle toiled i3lowly up a street that led out into the open eoun- trv. The ,mornin7, delae the ..wind and the chill, bega_ii to ha plct.,sa at. The clouds lilted, awl the sky brightened. Ilinda flaw through the air, and chirping., Or hopped over the green fiehs f.eareh of There were yong ).auths in the tvr.k,.l :411.i1Grvenci. already far advan-

div.head: BETWEEN INCOME AND OUTGO.
div.p: BETWEEN INCOME AND OUTGO.

Try to fancy this now. You awd I are standing side by side in some country place, on the shore or margin of a little pond. At one end of this pond there is an in- let, at the other an outlet. 'The water runs in,the water runs out, equally, evenly. The constant gain, the con- stant loss—with the pond—the product of both, lying quiet between. So nature balances all things, only you don't observe it.

Well, you say, what of it? Very much of it as you will see if you will read on a bit further. Here, for example, is a trifle of personal history told by a lady whose name will he found at the end of it. It is a *tory of pain at first. We naroe this so you can drop it now if you don't like such tales. But Feu would better go on with it.

She says she has—or had up to a certain date—suffered all her life from illness. Her feelings were the same as the feelings of millions—your own for aught we can tell. She felt tired, weary, and heavy. Her mind was bur- dened also, as if some coming evil had cast its shadow before. Her skin was sallow,a.nd the whites of her eyes turned yellow. She had an abiding sense of sickness at the stomach, pain in the right side, and spat up a watery fluid. She had no desire for food, and when (as must be) she took any, it seemed t,) cause pain and tightness .t the chest and under the shoulder blades.

This was often so bad that the poor woman actually regarded her molls with terror, as though bread and meat were deadly poisons, intead of being among the most precious gifts of God ;sa lot days together she fasted through fear of them.

From this came weakness, of course, we see. She could hardly pull herseif upstairs, and her breathing was short and laboured. After a little she got nervous and irritable. and treinlill and ;,hook all over, so she says, and we t!elieve it easily enough. At night whets we all ought to he sound asleep and sweetly dreaming, this woican tossed and tumbled on her bed. There was no gentle spirit tfa seal her lids,and. so she felt More tired in the morning than when she lay down hours before. Time ticked along and brought no comfort nor better- ment. She took medicines, lots of them, but couldn't point to any good they did. Doctors ? To be sure. Its always that way. The doctors have the first chance to show what they can do. " I consulted several doc- tors," said the lady. Did they help her ? They should, it's their business. Alas however !
In this ease they failed, as they so oft.in fail. " They gave me no relief," the tells us. Why Int ?

Her narrative conc!udes thus ; " On August 18th,1887 whilst living at v.:aki'field-street, Gray's Inn Road, 'I went to tile Royal Free Hospital .trni was und!?r treat- ment there for six weeks. Afterwards in 1383, I at. tended the Waterloo-road liospitol as an outdoor tatient for two months. Several doctors there said I was suffering froin liver complaint, but their phOic (2;4 not do ine the slightest good. In this condition I continued until August, 1889, when I made my first trial of Mother Seigel'S Curative Syrup. The first bottle relieved me, and I kept on tak- ing it. Soon my food agreed with me nod I knew no more sickness or nervime,ness. My spirits were good and I felt better than ever I did in my life. From that time I have had no return of my old complaint. I will gladly answer any inquiries. Yours truly, (sb:ned 'Mrs.) Annie Palmer, 9, Lambeth Palace-road, London, S.E., July 18th, 18D2." Wife of Mr. E. Palmer, Grocer and Provision D..:a!er.

One word more about that pond.. The human body is like it, beim: composed of, and sustained by, the food we eat, When the food is properly digested, and the usQless portions carned away through the organs of let, we are in health. Wrien either fads we fall and may die. This !ailmeis indigeAion, and dyspepsia.. was Mrs. Palmer's ailment, which the doctors treqtEd-,in vain and Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup cured. This. medicine helps natun to resrore. her lost ugutlibriutn, leaving the body tafe and strong between its income and its out;;;o.

With a view to direct the attention of agriculturists and others to a special industry for which there seems to be room for development lin various parts. of the country, the !fond !if Agriculture have directed ,their inspectors, Mr. W. C. Little and Mr. J. Brown, of Wis- hed). to prepare a report on the cultivation of .aisiers for baika making in the Fen districts. Their report is issued in the form of a lealt,t, to be obtained at Messrs. Eyre and Spottiswoode's, In nearly every country in , Europe osiers are grown to a more or less considerable extent, and good profits are believed Li, be obtained from this cultivation. There are no official records of the quantity of Osiers irarp4rted into this eturntry but it has heel) estimated that some thowoncis at tons are re- ceived from abroad annually. There is also said to be a large and increasing importation of baskets. The number of baskets required tor the fruit industry alone is con- siderable. and it must increase with the exten.,,ion of I fruit cultivation. A LLEC-ED BURIAL SCANDAL AT MOORE.
DROWNED MAN INTERRED IN HIS CLOTHES.
EXTRA ORDINARY CASE.

At the Runcorn Board of Guardians on Tuesday' aft7h.noon, Mr. J. Mc Intyre presiding, Mr. Samuel- Wood,vard, guardian for Kingsley, made reference to a report of a man who was found drowned at, Moore, having been buried with his clothes on, including his hat and clogs, and without having been washed or receiving any kindly act. Such a. proceeding nx4lo one wonder whether we were living in the 19th century, and in a land of civilization. It- seemed to him that some explanation should be given as to who was responsible for dealing with the dead body of a mm in such ama nner. The question was alto- gether a very vexed one as it was almost indecent to so dispose of a body_ rhe Clerk said that if a mai,' was found drowned he would be buried on the certificate of a coroner.

Mr. Woodward stated that then came the question of burial through their officer, and if so, should not a man be bUried in a respectable manner. He asked that ques- tion On ttieiall of those who believed themselves to be the representatives of the man referred to, who had only hear 4 about the matter since he was buried. No des- cription had been given of him. He was found on the Bth March and evidently within a few minutes of getting into the water for the body was warm and efforts were made at restoration. It was kept four days and then buried, under the circumstances mentioned, in Dares, bury Churchyard on the 12th March. The friends of a man missing we,e not perfectly satisfied for they had bad no infortnation except the police description and they were intending to ask for the exhumation of the body. To bury it in that style was quite repugnant to their feelings. Mr. Stokes suggested that Mr. De Prez, the relieving officer, might give them more information in the matter.

Mr. De PrPz in answer to questions said he could not say anything further than that the man was buried. Ha did not see him between giving the order and the burial.. The undertaker who carried out the order had conducted previous interments without complaints being made of him. He learned afterwards that two men from Run- conn had identified the body by a nick-name, but they did not communicate with him.. His responsibility went so far as burying and paving expenses. The over- seers had nothing to Co with it. It was the first intima- tion he had received that the man had been buried in his cloqiin,g.. It was not his intention that such a thing should have occurred. He paid quite sufficient for him to be buried in a proper and respectable manner. The, clothing on the body was worthless, he had been told. The Rev.. J. Hanby pointed out that the police gener- ally took charie of the clothing in such cases for the purposes of identification. Mr. Lea confirmed this opinion.. _ . _

Mr. De Prez remarked that he was one of the jory- men at the inquest, but the jury did not view the body. Mr. Woodward expressed surprise at hearing such a statement, and said that seeing that the man had died violently how could a jury pronounce a verdict upon a body winch they bad never examined ? The Rev. J. Hanby said they had to pay for the funeral, and therefore to a certain extent, they were re- sponsible. The statement made by Mr. De Prez as to. not viewing the body was a very grave one, and he thought that the only course was to communicate to the, Home Secretary. Mr. Woodward thought there was not the slightest doubt that such a course would be adopted, as i was. intended to apply for an order for exhumation. Mr. Stokes considered that some inquiries should be. made from the police._ . . . _

Mr. Heywood remarked that it was not the duty of that Board to determine whether juries should view bodies. The cp-iestion at issue was whether the body had, been interred in an indecent manner or otherwise. Fle proposed that Mr. De Prez sift the matter during next fortnight and communicate the result to the Board at its next meeting.—This proposition was seconded and carried.

div.head: ItOUBILLAC AND JOHNSON.
div.p: ItOUBILLAC AND JOHNSON.

Once, while Roubillac was engaged on the Nightin- gale monument, a messenger found him plungeo in a. fit of obstraction before one of the kneeling figures in- the adjacent tomb of Sir Francis 'Were. " Hush !"—he- whispered mysteriously,when his attention was at length aroosed,—" hush ! he vii speak presently." Upon an- other occasion, being pre-occupied with his own concep- tion of •MrNightineale,he suddenly dropped his knife and. fork at dinner, and flung himself into an attitude of horror whiclralmost petrified the luckless serving boy at whom his looks appeared to be directed. Something of the same restless and impulsive extravagance no doubt pa.sed into and exaggerated his manner of speaking. There is a story says Austin Dobson in " The Magazine' of Art," that when he wanted an inscription for one of his Westminster efforts, Reynolds accompanied him to Johnson's famous Gough Square garret. Roubillac- straightway began a full-blown and highly-seasoned har- angue in order to explain his errand. But the big man was down ripen him instanter, Lidding him bluntly kin Falstaff phrase) " deliver himself like a man ot this world."' " Come, come, sir," said he in his most magis- terial manner, " let as have no more or this bombastic,. ridiculous rhodomontade. Let me know, in simple. language, the name, character, and q.ualit7 of the person who.3e epitaph you intend to have me write."

MONDAY.

In the House of Commons on Monday evening Mr. A. MOBLEY, replying to questions, said the points of differ- ence between the telephone companies and the Post office had been brought within such narrow compaSS that he believed the agreement would be laid on the table very shortly. Mr. AFQIIITH moved for leave to bring in a bill to amend the law relating to factories and workshops. Among other things, the bill places further limits on the working of overtime, restricts the employment outside factories of children, women, and young persons also employed inside, treats steam laundries as factories,and other laundries as workshops, and extends the scope of the" particulars" clause to the Factory Act of 1891. The right hon.gentlerna.n expressed a hope that the mea- sure might be referred to the Standing Committee on Trade. The motion was agreed to, and the bill was brought in and read a first time. The debate on the motion for leave to introduce the Welsh Disestablishment Bill Was resumed by Mr. Lloyd- George, who after quoting statistics to disprove the statement that Nonconformists were a decaying force, while the church was increasing in numbers, said the bill was accepted by the Welsh people as a highly state- manlike measure, lont there was a strong feeling against the coinpensatpn clause, and if passed in its present shape the bill would intensify the causes of disturbance. Mr. Bryce wound lip the debate, and the bill was read a Ilrst time without a division. The second reading was formally fixed for Monday next. The Shop Hours Act Amendment Bill was read a second time.

div.head: LIBERALISM IN THE WIDNES DIVISION. MR. 11. WADE DEACON ON THE WELSII DISESTABLISHMENT BILL.
div.p: LIBERALISM IN THE WIDNES DIVISION. MR. 11. WADE DEACON ON THE WELSII DISESTABLISHMENT BILL.

On Tuesday evening, a public meeting of Liberals was held at the Liberal Club, Alford-et., Widnes, for the purpose of ap.poinling the execu- tive and district councils for the borough for the ensuing year. Mr. E. Carey presided, being sup- ported on the platform by Mr. 11. Wade Deacon, Alderman Wareing, Mr. S. Deacon, Mr. H. B. Shores , (Liberal agent), &e. The Chairman, in opening tke proceedings, said that so far as their Government had gone, they as Liberals and Radicals had every reason to be thoroughly satis- fied. Their opponents had, he thought, done the party a great deal of good on several occasions.. Under the present law a large number of working me m and com- mercial men were deprived of their votes. This they had always considered a very great hardship, and the new bill would do a Ist to remove the griemance. He however, did not see that a man who moved about from one town to another in search of work should be des- cribed as a vagrant by Lord Salisbury, There were also the ministers of the Wesleyan body, who under present conditions could not in the great majority of cases obtain their votes, and these also, he supposed, came wader ;Lord Salisbury's definition. Alderman Wareing moved a resolution expressing re- gret at Mr. Gladstone's retirement, welcoming Lord Rose- bery as his successor, and trusting that the Government svould press forward the many beneficent reforms desired by the Liberal party. , Mr. F. Hartland seconded the resolution, and

H. Wade Deacon, in supporting, referred to the Rouse of Lords. He said that se far as he knew (with the exception of the Marriage with the Deceased Wife's Sister Bill), the House of Lords had not during the last fifty years thrown out a bill sent up by a Tory Govern- ment., .but when a Liberal Government was in power every bill sent up was mutilated, mauled, or rejected. He did not pledge himself to any particular plan with reference to the House of Lords. He was not in favour of mending the House of Lords, because if they reformed it they would strengthen its power. The House of Lords should not, he thought, have the absolute veto, as they had at present, and this veto should be removed. Mr. Deacon then referred to the various measures passed last session il:ry the Government, and those introduced this session. Sir William Harcourt was, he said, to be congratulated upon introducing an exceedingly able Budget. h. new era had begun in their system of taxa- tion. Referring to the Welsh Disestablishment Bill, he said the introduction of the bill proved that the Liberal party was doing its utmost to fulfil its pledges. It was a bill which would try them to the very bottom. They might regret that the Welsh people were not Church- men, hut he thought the Welsh people had a right to judge for themselves in the matter, and whem they found that thirty-one out of the thirty-four representAtivea of Wales were pledged to the disestablishmertt of the church he thought the people were entitled to it. He would support the bill on those grounds. He did not think that the cause of religion would suffer if the hill was passed, nor did he think that the Church in England would be any weaker. ff the day ever did arrive—and he personally hoped the day was far off—when there was such an opinion in fay.ur of disestablishment in England. the people would have their demands granted, hut. until that time did arrive he believed that the church of Erigis.nd would be as strong as ever after the Church in Wales had been Risestablislird.
The election of officer.; v..ai; then proceeded with, and a vote of tanks to the Chairman concluded the pro- ceelipgs.

div.head: TUESDAY.
div.p: TUESDAY.

In the House of Commons on Tuesday evening, Mr. S. SMITH called attention to the remark made by the Re- corder of Liverpool in a recent case to the effect that it did not matter whether the jury found the prisoner guilty or not guilty, as he should only sentence her to one day's imprisonment. Mr. AscaniTz said he had re- ceived an explanation en the subject from Mr. Hopwoou who told him that he regretted the observation as soon as he had made it. Mr. AsQuint informed Mr. Knatchbull-Hugessen that ! there was no intention to int.erfere with the use-of the cathedrals in Wales, and so long as the Church Body so desired they would continue to ne applied to the present services and no others. On the motion for the second reading of the Registra- tion Bill Sir E. CLARKE moved an amendment declining to proceed further with a bill effecting extensive changes in our representative system in the absence of proposals for the redress of the inequalities existing in the distri- bution of electoral power. Sir C. DELKE said that when the right time came they would all be in favour of a fur- ther redistribution of SratS, but the Conservative party were very much mistaken if they thought that the prin- ciple of equal electoral districts, and one vote one value would benefit them. Mr. Drsp.sam spoke against a Saturday poll. The debate was adjourned at mid- night. WEDNESDAY.

In the House of Commons on Wednesday, Mr. Bartley moved the second reading of the Church Patronage Bill, the objects of which, he said, were to stop the sale by public auction of next presentations to livings, to stop traffic in livings, and to give the bishop of the diocese some power to prevent improper persons from being instituted to benefices: Sir W. Harcourt did not. oppose the second reading, but said he thought the bill did not deal in anything like an adequate way with the matters•concerned. The people who had a right to a voice in the Appointment of a min- ister were the congregation. En the course of his speech Sir WiLuam remark,d that the strength of the Church was in the towns and not in the icountry parishes, this being due to the fact that the churches in the towns were really voluntary churches. Toe amendment was negatived without a division, and the bill was read a second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Law. Mr. E. SPENCER moved the second reading of a bill to establish a Ministry of Labour. Eir Charles Dilke and Lord Randolph Churchill objected to the appointanent of new Ministers, and Mr. Asquith, on behalf of the Government, opposed the bill, the second reading of which was negatived without a division. Mr. VINCENT moved the second reading of the Foreign Goods (Mark of Origin) Bill, which was intended, he said, to remedy defects in the Merchandise Marks Act of 1887, under which goods could come into this country unmarked. Mr. Mundella condemned the measure as absurd, and said it was nothing but protection. Mr. Havelock Wilson, Mr. Godson, Mr.-Muntz, Mr. Warner, and Mr. T. Bowles supported the bill, and Sir J. Joicey, Mr. Roby, and Mr. G. W. Palmer opposed it. Sir J. Rigby said the existing law was sufficient to prevent the import of goods having any false description as to their place of origin. On a division there voted for the second reading 157; against, 183; majority against, 26.

div.head: WARUNGTON AND THE EEN'S VISIT
div.p: WARUNGTON AND THE EEN'S VISIT
TO THE SHIP CANAL.

At a meeting of the Town Council on Tuesday evening, Councillor BENNETT said he wished to refer to a matter of considerable urgency. What was the final decision of the Queet with reference to the visit to the Ship Canal? Was there any possible chanch of inducing her Majesty to stop at Warrington? (A Voice "No.";, Would the Council be represented at the opening of the Canal, and were any steps being taken to consult their dignity as a Corporation on the occasion? All these were questions which effected the dignity if not the welfare of Warringtcn. They ought not to sit idly by and allow these questions to go by default. In the interests of the public, something definite ought to be known about the •matter. (Hear. hear.) Were their interests being looked after by the General Purposes Committee'? The TOWN CLERK, at the request of the Mayor, ex- lained that a fortnight age they were both in London, and they called on Mir. Robert Pierpoint, M.P., and told him their wishes in the matter. They represented that Warrington as a loyal town wished to present an address to the Queen, and they were, therefore, anxious to know what arrangements had been made in connection with the visit of the Queen to the Ship Canal. Mr. Pierpoint saw I,erd Cross on the following day, and he advised the Mayor to write to Sir Flenry Ponsonliy.Flis Worship did so, and riceived a reply stating that the arrangements were to the effect that her Majesty would visit Manchester, but that he did net think be would stop at Warrington. Everytking had been done that could be done to persuade her to do so, but he (the Town Clerk) could quite under- stand that it would require deep persuasion to induce the Queen to alter her arrangements to meet the wishes of the people of Warrington. Councillor BENNETT : Would not a resolution of the Council induce her to make a call at Warrington. The TOWN CLERK: Lord Cross assured us that nothing would persuade her Majesty to alter her arrangements with regard to Warrington. We have not yet received any invitation from the Ship Canal Company with regard to the visit to Manchester. Councillor BENNETT : Cannot we do anything with reference to it?
The TOWN CLERK : I don't think we should ask for an invitation. (Hear, hear.) Alderman BuTcunisoN : What is the programme ? _
. . The TOWN CLERIC: I have heard—it is only a news- paper report—that the Queen will go straight to Man- chester. _ _ _
The minutes were confirmed and the Council rose.

div.head: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES- W ARRINGTON.
div.p: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES- W ARRINGTON.
WYCLIFFE SUNDAY bCHOOL ANNIVERSARY.

This annual vent in connection with the above-named Sunday school, took place on Sunday, and may be said to have been one of the most successful of recent years. There were large congregations, those in the afternoon and evening being very large indeed. The Rev. J. A. Mitchell, 8.A., of St. Helens, was the preacher, and his discourses were listened to with much interest, and greatly appreciated. At the morning service,besides the usual sermon, he delivered a short address to the scho- lars, taking as his text "Learn of Me." He urged them to be bright, obedient, gentle, and cheerful. He chose as his text for the sermon, "That it may give seed to the sower and bread to the eater : so shall My Word be," Isaiah 55c. 10 and 11 verses. The singing of the children was particularly good, and the anthem "Break forth into joy" was well sung by the choir. Mrs. R. H. Pearson admirably rendered a solo "Jerusalem." At the usual P.S.A. meeting in the afternoon the scholars were admitted, and were accommodated around the pulpit. They sang the same hymns as at the morning service,and Mrs. R. H. Pearson again sang "Jerusalem." Mr. S. B. Stringer was the Chairma.n,and took aa his subject "How can we make life happy ?" The Rev.J.A.. Mitchell, 8.A., delivered the address,and spoke upon the importance of making the best possible use of opportunities,in both tem- poral and spiritual matters,as they could not count upon having them repeated. Messrs.T Wallington,R.Atkinson, and W. H. Bailey also took part in the service. The even- ing service commenced by the choir singing the anthem "Lighten our darkness." During the service the choir also sang the anthem "Sing unto the Lord with thanks- giving," in which Mrs. R. H. Pearson and Miss F. Booth were very effective in the parts allotted them. Mr. W. H. Wallington sang the solo "Nazareth" in his usual excellent manner. The preacher delivered a powerful discourse from the words contaimed in the Ist and 2nd verses of Isaiah 40th chapter. Mr. G.Wallington, super- intendent of the Sunday school,had charge of the musical arrangements. Mr. W. H. Payton presided at the organ with his usual ability. The collections for the day amounted to £ ELLESMERE-STREET WESLEYAN MISSION.

The first anniversary in connection with this Mission took place on Sunday, when services were held in the afternoon and evening. The afternoon service was con- ducted by Mr. Sandford. Solos were given by Miss Wheatley and Mr. Fieldhouse, and quartettes by the Misses Gornall and Rawlin, and Messrs. bonier and Fieldhouse. Mr. Walter Brough.w as the preacher at the evening service. There were good congregations, and a satisfactory amount was realized by the collections. The annual meeting was held on Monday evening and was preceded by a tea. There was not a very large attend- ance. The chair was occupied by Mr. J.' B. Isaac. After singing and prayer by the Rev. J. Gunnell, Mr. Isaac Barlow gave his report. He said they celebrated that day the opening of their new building there, and he thought; taking all things into consideration that they had not been very lazy during the past twelve months. They had done what they could to get the young people to rally round them, and they had to some extent been very successful. Their Sunday school was now on very lrood lines, and that was a very important branch which , they were all very well aware of. It was the hope of their mission. They had a band of teachers as good as lany other in the circuit, and they had 309 scholars. When they thought of the time when they inaugurated the school, and when they only had 20 or 30 scholars as a nucleus, he thought they were to be con- gratulated, considering that they had had all their scholars from that neighbourhoodiand many of them had never attended Sunday school before. (Applause.) Another pleasing feature in connection with their school was the number of young people in the society class, Which he considered was a very hopeful sign. They had had one or two meetings during the winter in connection with their Band of Hope, the membership of which was about 80. Another branch in connection with the Sun- day school which was very important was the penny bank, to encourage thrift amongst the children and their parents. (Applause.) They had close upon 198 members on their penny bank books. When they left the old Buttermarket-street school their members numbered 42. The money was distributed very six months, at Christ- mas and Walking Day, and in June next they hoped to be able to distribute over £3O. The Society class was in a very thriving and prosperous condition, and there were 60 members on the books. The speaker afterwards referred to the success of the recreative and instruction classes, and the Saturday evening penny concerts which had been held in the Mission Room during the winter season. Speaking of the bazaar which had been held during the year in aid cf the mission, he said they had been enabled to pay over £lOO towards the liquidation of the debt on the mission.—Mr. J. B. Isaac addressed the meeting, after which Miss B. Dutton referred to the memorial which had been erected in Westminster Abbey to commemorate the life of Jenny Lind, and 'afterwards related an incident which had come under her own observation, showing the value of individual effort. In conclusion she hoped they would go on prospering in their work at the Mission.—The Rev. Owen Watkins spoke of his early experiences in Christian work in the hack streets of Manchester, and humorously described the, converting of a dancing room into a Methodist Chapel.—The Rev. J. Malan thought that the year had been a year of progress in every direction in connection with the Mission. He hoped they would go on prosper- ing and that during the coming year they would have greater results. Refering to the financial position of the Mission he said they had only a debt of £lOO, and per- haps,in two years that would be paid off. Mr.L.Richard- son presided at the harmonium, and also sang a solo.

The House Committee reported that Mr. S. Davies had been elected chairman, and Mr. E. Aukland vice- chairman of the committee, and the Schools Committee also reported that they had elected Mr. W. Houghton chairman, and Mr. S. Davies, vice-chairman of the corn- mittee for the ensuing year.

div.head: WARDS QUESTION.
div.p: THE WARDS QUESTION.

Mr. RATCLIFFE said that the people of Newton were desirous of appealing to the County Council, through the Guardians to have a member for each ward upon the District Camel!. Ihey did not wish to be behind hand on Nov. Bth.—The Clerk replied that the Guardians had already affirmed the principle of having a Guardian for each ward, and it would be better for Newton to apply on their own behalf by means of the Commissioners or through the overseers of the township.—Mr.Ratcliffe re- torted that the Commissioners had nothing to do with the question, and that the people of Newton were desir- ous that the Guardians should support them.—The Clerk said that it would be best to apply through the overseers.—The meeting then terminated.

div.head: PULPIT PARAPHERNALIA. SCREWING THE PARSON UP.
div.p: PULPIT PARAPHERNALIA. SCREWING THE PARSON UP.

There are fashions, it seems, in pulpits, and many of them, to judge by Mr. Langston's article in '6 The Argosy." This reverend gentleman t3lls a story of a vicar of a Cheshire parish where he was about to preach who had invented a contrivance on the screw principle, by which the clerk could either raise or lower the floor of the pulpit to any level. During the hymn," said one who had had experience of this ap- paratus, " I felt myself screwed ' for the first time, and the idiot did not stop until my knees were visible ; when, seeing his mistake, I came down with a run which did not lessen the too audible titter or my own confusion and fright." In another instance, three dis- used hassocks gave the occupant of the pulpit the proper elevation. These proved so unsteady that he was obliged to grasp the pulpit ledge with one hand,and during the sermon, needing this to find a reference, the top hassock glided backwards, and he suddenly dis- appeared with a bang, Bible and all. An amusing arrangement is stated to be still existing at St. James' Church, Bath. Before the sermon, the pulpit, a veri- table Jack-in-the-box, is wheeled to the east end cf the nave, and after the 6' fifthly" has been disposed of, is duly trundled back again.

LORD ROSEBERY met with a mag- Lordancheste Roseberr. at v nificent reception at Manchester M on Wednesday, and his speech was worthy of the immense crowd of Lancashire Liberals who had assembled to hear him. Ho dealt at some length with three of the most vital questions of the present time,namely, Home Rule, the reform of the methods of procedure of the House of Commons, and the need for binding together in one powerful party all the friends of progress in the country. It as been said that Lord ROSEBERY has no belief in Home Rule, and that he is prepared to throw it overboard on the first opportune occasion. Sach insinuations aro in the highest degree malicious when viewed in connection with the fact that his lordship has just succeeded to the leadership of the Liberal party, and after the speech at Man- chester their absurdity must be apparent to the most bigotted partisan. Lord ROSEBERY is, it is clear, not only a Home Ruler, but a Home Ruler of the most convinced and co nvi naing type. With him Home Rule is accepted as an inevit- able development of the political constitution of the country. As he points out, Home Rule was not originated with Mr. GLADSTONE'S Bill of 1886; it was a necessary consequence of the extension of the franchise two years prior to that date. Those Liberals who object to the principle of Irish self- gove rnment, apart from the mere details of the Bill giving effect to it, made their stand too late when they waited till 1886. Their resistance should have begun when the extension of the franchise was first mooted. To first give the Irish people power to elect a sufficient number of mem- bers to enforce their de mends, or to bring the Parliamentary machine to a standstill, and then to Ore a point blank refusal to the demands of those members after they have received a mandate from their constituents is both illogical and un- reasonable. Lord ROSEBERY'S politics are not of that wrong-headed typo. Ho does not believe in the kind of statesmanship which consists in one day giving the people power to shape their own destinies and the next day trying to prevent them exercising that power. It is sufficient for him that the Irish people demand Home Rule, and that it can be conceded to them with advantage so far as the unity and the stability of the Empire as a whole are con- cerned. No better foundation for a faith in Home Rule and for a determination to see that it is carried through need be required. The language which the Premier used in regard to the House of Commons was both timely and significant. There can be no question that the House is becoming a very inefficient instrument for the effecting of legislation. Rules of proce- dure which permit any insignificant member to put a stop at midnight to any measure, no matter how uncontentious or important it may be, are certainly in need of amendment. Lord ROSEBERY referred particu- larly to the " veto " that had been put upon Mr. MUNDELLA'S conciliation bill by a single member who had never given any reason for doing so. The member referred to is DO doubt MT. ROBERT PIERPOINT who, we believe, misrepresents the workingmen of Warrington in this matter, as he does in others. Mr. PlaarorarT may now plume himself on having attained some distinction by stopping useful legislation ; he can certainly claim no credit for promoting it. Another istance of the mis-use of the power which the rules of the House of Commons leaves in the hands of private and comparatively irresponsible private members is found in the blocking of the Bill which would prevent the working of shop assistants more than eleven hours a day. In concluding his speeech, Lord ROSEBERY made a strong appeal to all pro- gressive politicians to close their ranks, and to discountenance sectional efforts which would only result in weakening the main party. The alter- native, as he carefully pointed out, means Tory dominance for many years to come.

Tins is the title of a hook which "The English- is of moro than usual interest to man at Home." 'Warringtonians, seeing that its author, MT. EDWARD PORRITT, is a native of the "good old town," though now resident in the United States. The book, which is published by Messrs. Putnam's Sons, of London and New York, is a handsomely printed and substantially bound volume of close upon four hundred pages. MT. Portnr.rfs primary object has been to descrilyz the municipal and national institutions 0.,f Eng- land for the instruction of Americans, but it is no exaggeration to say that his book contains in- formation that would be fresh and useful to nit ety- nine out of every hundred Englishmen. The machinery and methods of English local self-govern- ment are dealt with fully and lucidly,and there are several chapters devoted to such subjects as Poor- law administration, Parliament and its work, the administration of justic, taxation, the State , departments, the Church and IN-in-conformity, the naval and military services, labour legisla- tion, the land laws and the Press. Although Mr. PORRITT disclaims being either a lawyer or an expert, his writings clearly indicate that his experiences as it press- man—in th., first place as a reporter in this die- tr:ct, and afterwards as the London representl- tiv.: of daily newspapers—brought him into close and livin7 contact with the various phases of both national and ioctl institutions. It is interesting to note that i s • veral instances the illustrations are drawn from the airairs of what is described as a typical English town of between forty and fifty
