Mr. PORRITT can certainly be congratulated on having turned his knowledge to a very useful purpose in compiling the" Englishman at Home," which will, we should think, considering its accu- racy and completeness become a standard book of its kind in America.

AT the meeting last week in The Clergy th an,dconnection with the Police Court e " Trade.' and Prison Gate Mission the Rector of Warrington alluded to the charges sometimes made that the Church is "tongue-tied" in regard to the evils of the liquor traffic. It does not seem very clear whether Mr. WILLIs's inten- tion was to refute these charges, but if so he signally failed. In fact, he practically substan- tiated them. The allegations in this respect against the Church amount to this, that while the clergy recognise and often openly acknow- ledge and deplore the immense evils which spring from the liquor trade as it is now carried on they make no effectual or whole-hearted efforts to remove the causes. This indifterence is ascribed to the fact that the brewers are generous in their benefactions to the Church. Mr. WILLIS said nothing that could have any tendency to remove these impressions. He admitted that drink is the great cause ef the crime and misery we see around us, and, at the same time, he thankfully and publicly acknowledged that he received help from the' local brewcrs whose trade is the source of this same crime and misery. It is true that he propounded or suggested certain remedies in the shape of restriction upon the trade, but it is just at this point where the weakness of the clergy as temperance reformers is manifested. How are these restrictions to be effected ? Clearly, there is only one way, and that is by legislation. Are the clergy of the established Ch urch conspicuous in their support of the politicians who are in favour of restricting the drink traffic? That question can only be answered with a decided negative. They deplore the evils of the traffic,they suggest restriction, and—they vote and use their influence in favour of men who fight tooth and nail against anything in the nature of restric- tion.

FORTHCOMING DEPARTURE FROM RUNCORN OF INSPECTOR COOPER.

In consequence of the death of Superintendent Walker of the police division of Altrincham, and also of the retirement of Superintendent Leah, of Nantwich, many changes in the stations of the various police officers in the Cheshire constabulary are reported. Amongst these is the intended transfer of Inspector Cooper from R un- corn to Crewe. This latter gentleman, who has been stationed in Runcorn for more than two years has won the respect and esteem of everyone with whom he has come into contact during his comparatively short reii- dence in the town ,and his departure will certainly create a general expression of regret, nikngled with pleasure at his having been chosen for a more important station in the country. That he will leave this district with the well wishes of the inhabitants there is no doubt. His departure, it is expected will be made in the course of next week or of the following one. JOSEPH PRITCHARD. Watchmaker and Jeweller, Si, Nigh- it., Ituncorn.—Advt.

TISE RUNCORN FIRE BRIGADE: A SMART "TURN OUT." On Thursday Mr. R. Wright, superintendent of the Runcorn Volunteer Fire Brigade, determined to discover if the members of the brigade could distinguish the sound of his" blower" from those heard on vessels proceeding along the Ship Canal. It had often been remarked that the squnds of those used by the Ship Canal craft and the one used .by Mr. R. Wright to warn the firemen, were very similar, and that hardly any difference could be detected. As it was thought that this would prove very serious if an outbreak of fire occurred at night-time,Mr. Wright resolved to put it to the test and at 6.40 in the evening he sounded his blower in the customary way as though a fire had been notified. The, result was emin- ently satisfactory. One man arrived in two minureA, two more in three minutes, two in four, two in four and a quarter, aid three in five, so that at the end of fire minutes ten of the brigade were on the spot and ready to commence operations. BOATMAN DROWNED_ IN RUNCORN DOCKS.

- - . The body of a man named John Hanson, apparently about the age of 52 years, flatman, of Brighouse, York- shire, was found on Thursday morning at three o'clock in the tidal dock, Runcorn. From particulars to hand it appears that Hanson had charge of the fiat "Richard," owned by the Rochdale Canal Company. Late on Wednesday night he and his son were to4ether on board as the boat was being berthed. Hanson told his son to go below and he would see the craft safely docked. The sr,Jn, Beaumont Hanson, did so and went to sleep. At three o'clock he was awakened and surprised to find that his father was not bul.xw and becoming apprehensive he raised an alarm, and with the assistance of a young man named John Inman, began to drag the dock with irons. They were not long before the body was re- covered and not far away from it was a long hook usei on board the boat which lead to the supposition that the man had fallen overboard as he was pushing the boat. The circumstances have been communicated to the Coroner who will hold an inquest to-day (Friday).

CRILDREN'S CONCERT AT THE BETHESDA LECTURE HALL,

RUNCORN. On Wednesday evening an entertainment was given in the Bethesda Lecture Hall,Runcorn, by the members of a children's class, which has been conducted, during the winter months, by the Rev. John Simpson. Mr. Joseph Speakman occupied the chair. A lengthy programme. consisting of solos, duets, recitations and dialogues, was gene through by the children in the most praiseworthy mariner. One of the most inc.eresting features in the evening's proceedings was the distribution of 48 elegantly bound books, which had been provided by Mr. Simpson as prizes to the children for regular attendance and good reproductions of the addresses delivered by him during ! the season. Be remarked that seine of the compositions were really wonderful when it was considered how young the children were. The ceremony of distributing the hooks was performed by Mrs. Cameron, who congratulated the recipients upon their successes. Towards the close of the entertainment,votes of thanks were accorded Mrs. Cameron, Miss Johnson Mr. Speakman, Mr. Simpson, and others. In respond- ing Mr. Speakman said he had experienced much enjoy- ment that evening from the children's performances which had given him the grea,or.; satisfaction. The manner in which they had all gone t Tough their respec- tive items spoke well for the ability of the children and also reflected much credit upon Mr. Simpson and his helper. Miss Lillie Johnson, both of whom had prepared the children for the evening.—Mr. Simpson ira acknow- ledgment said the class had always been a great source of pleasure to him and he was heartily thankful of the 1 appreciation shown by the audience.

div.head: L VEXED QUESTION.
div.p: L VEXED QUESTION.

Mr. Brandreth said that at the last meeting a com- mittee was appointed to inquire into the action of the Board's Relieving Officer for Runcorn district, Mr. Cooke, in dealing with a case in which a man named Thomas Curzon was concerned. That committee had met on the previous Monday with himself (Mr. Bran- dreth) in the chair. Mrs. Curzon, Dr. Robinson, and his assistaet were present, and their statements bore out the one made by Mr. T. Cooke, which was read at the last meeting of the Board. There were a few fresh particulars obtained which showed that Mrs. Curzon, whilst at her brother's house, had earned 53. ner week and her food by nursing; and fri. 63. and food per day by washing. She had been able to keep herself and her children. She further stated that Mr. Percival, the Commissioner's Nuisance Inspector, had told her she should seek relief for the children. The testimony of Dr. Robinson was to the effect that the cottage where Curzon lived was much the seine as others. Curzon was in bed when Dr. Robinson saw him and appeared to be properly lodged and cared for. It was partly on account of the infectious di3ease, partly that his wife might continue her oecupatiou, and partly that when convalescent he might have better nourishment, that he (the doctor) recommended the man's removal to the hospital. If the man lied not been removed lie should have continued to attend him until some other medical man took the case over, and he would have given him the same attention as his other patients. Concluding, Dr. Robinson remarked : "I have generally • been received by other officials in an official manner, but I have always found Mr. Cooke very different, and very ready to listen to any statements in any Case I have had occasion to speak to him about it." Mr. Bran- dreth, continuing, said, that th 4 Cemmittee were thoroughly satisfied that. Mr. Cook had done all that was necessary, that the man was not destitute, that he was properly lodged and cared for, and that he was re- ceiving proper medical treatment. They were also of the opinion that Mr. Percival sent Mrs. Curzon te the Relieving Officer, to obtain, if possible, a medical order, thinking that if one was given, the man would be pauperised, and that being a pauper, the cost of his maintenance in the hospital would fall upon the Guar- dians of the Union, and not upoa the Urban Sanitary Authority. Further, that Mrs. Curzon would not have applied lo the Relieving Officer at all if she had not been sent by Mr. Percival. They therefore unanimously en- dorsed the action of the Relieving Officer. He (Mr. Brandreth) begged to move the adoption of the report. Mr. Heywood seconded the adoption.—Mr. Taylor thoueht that if a copy of a letter for the Commissioners referring the same case had been received by the Guar- dians from the Local Government Board it should be - read before the report was adopted.—The Clerk did not concur with this opinion.—Mr. Taylor pressed his argu- ment, contending that nothing was before the meeting, and that it was not a propsr course to take.—Mr. Bran- dreth considered that they were quite right in the course they were pursuing, as it was only the report of the Committee that they had before them.—After some dis- cussion the report was confirmed. The Clerk then reporttd a letter from the Local Gov- ernment Board, written on the 27th April and accom- panied by a letter received from the Runcorn . Improvement Commissieners. The Local Government Board asked for the ebservations of the Guardians thereon. The enclosed letter from the Commissioners to the Local Government Board was as' foLows :—" I am directed by the Health Committee of the Runcorn Improvement Commissioners to put the following par- ticulars before you, relative to a man named James Curzon, who was removed a short time ago to the hospital. Our Sanitary Inspector received an intimation from the medical practitioner ire the town, that this , inan Curzon was suffering from typhoid fever, and was • a fit case for removal to the hospital. The medical practitioner at the same time intimated that he should not continue his atteedence on him. The Sanitary Inspector on inquiry found tha t the man was quite des. titute, and that he was in a co nditiora of abselute want, and recommended his wife to make application to the Relieving Officer for an order for medical assistance. This she did. The woman's words were 'I told the relieving officer that I had not a penny in the world,and my husband was very bad with diarrhcea, and sick. We had two little children, the eldest 3 years, and the other 16 morales, and I had lived in Duke's Court, where I had to leave all my things far the rent, and that I had not a bed to lie upon. In answer to my request the relieving officer told rue if he was not removed that night, I was to go and see him on the following day at 2 o'clock and he would see Mr. Ashton (clerk to the Guardians). As my husband was very bad I went again the same even- ing, and asked him again for an order Le- medical attendance. The relieving officer then told me that he , was bound to be removed, and that those who took him would have to find medical attendance, or it would be a very serious affair for them. He told me to tell this to Mr. Percival, the sanitary inspector. I again told the relieving officer that I had not a penny in the world,that my husband might be dead before morning, and tint I had not a bed to lie upon. On my return to the Sanitary Inspector, I reported the result of my applica- tion to the relieving officer.' The Sanitary Inspector then went to see the relieving officer and alter some conversation the relieving officer also informed him that he would not give any order for medical assistance, and argued that it was the Health Gommittee's duty, and not his, as relieving officer, to provide medical assistance, and whatever was requiree. The Sanitary Inspector then reported the matter to my Health Committee, and as the case seemed to be of such a serious nature, demanding immediate attention, and as the relieving officer declined to move in the matter. my committee decided to remove the man to the hoepi- tal which was done, and two or three days after his ad- mission he died. The Health Committee considered that this was a case in which the relieving officer should have dealt with, and given the urgently needed relief and medical assistance. This authority has an agreement with the Runcorn Board of Guardians with respect to the maintenance of pauper patients in the hospital, but to brine the cases within the terms of the agreement the agreement the patients must be removed at the request of the Guardians. . By declining through their officer to make such request the Guardians evade all. responsibility for the maintenance and medical' attendance of all per- sons within our district suffering frem infectious com- plaints who are not in a position to get these essentials for themselves. I am directed to ask the opinion of your Lordships ae to whether this was not a case which the relieving officer should have dealt with, and also as to whether the Guardians ought not to make good the ex- penses incurred by these authority in removing, main- taining, providing medical attendance, and burying the man in question."—Mr. Hr's-wood proposed that the re- port of the ,ommittee be sent in reply te the request of the Local Goverament B rant —Mr. Taylor understood that Mrs. Curzon had made a statement to Mr. Imison who took it down upon eager as she made it, word for word. Also that she was receiving relief from the officer within a couple of days after her husband's removal.— Mr. Norman thought that the committee's report con- tradicted to some extent the case for the commis- sioners regarding the etatements of the medical officer. It seemed to him to be the old vexed question of what was a pauper case and who was a pauper.—Mr. Aaron said he had asked Dr. Robinson if he would have attended the patient whether paid for it or not to which Dr. Robinson had replied that he would have donee—The Rev. Hanby thought that the woman had altered her, statement somewhat to the Committee regarding the amount she earned. He understood she had told the Board that she could earn lls, per week by washing. but she toldthe Committee about Be. or 9e.—Mr. Thos. Lea: She isatow receiving relief from the Union.—The Rev. Hanby: But. she ha. 3 not got her husband now.— Mr. Brandreth said that as far as he could understand the woman had been keeping herself and children for some time without assistance from her husband who had been a. somewhat worthless fellow. Dr. Robinson had said that. it. was fir better for the man to be removed frcm the rather crewded district in which he lived than to remain in the house. Ha considered that the Commis- sioners as beine the health authority for the district were responsible alone for the expenses incurred. He , would like to know whether the Health Committee charged for the patients who entered the hospital suffer- ing from any infectious disease, as he was given to under- stand that the authorities in other towns did not charge. They,, as Guardians, had no right to give relief to per- sons. who could get it free, and if the rich obtained adtnissinn free into the hospitals surely it would be un- fair to charge the Dann—Mr. Heywood proposed that the report should he accompanied by the clause showing that the women had kept herself, and that both should be sent to the Local Government Board.—This course was ultimately agreed to be taken.

MEDICAL OFFICER'S MONTHLY REPORT. Dr. McDougall reported that during the month nine- teen deaths had been registered one of which was an inquest case. In the corresponding month of last year twc.tity-seven deaths occurred.—Mr. Pritchard remarked that tha rate was singularly low, and Pointed to the healthy state of the town.—Dr. Mc- Dougall : The report speaks for itself.

Walker and Son for alterations to conveniences. _
On the proposition of Mr. Wiswalt, seconded by Mr. Bisbrown, the minutes were confirmed,
HEALTH COMMITTEE.

This committee recommended :—That Sergeant John T. Lea be appointed an ansistant inspector of common lodging-houses in the place of Sergeant Gosling. That notices be served on owners and occupiers of houses in Mason-street, Pennington's-row, Sutton-street, and Dutton's-cour, to abate certain nuisaoces, :And make various alterations, and that in the eveht of non-com- pliance with such rE,tices, legal proceedirws be taken. Mr. E. Imison, in proposing the adoptiou of the mien- tes,s.!id that the coma-ill-tee were dealing with s()In- pro- perty in oueot the oldest parts of the town,and with the co-operation of th owners he hoped the property would he mach) to met modern tyquireine:•lts. —Mr. Handley , expres.d the opinion that the racon4m,ndation referring to pr-p:-rte 1,2, anti 3, Pennington•ro W, should a nended with reard to the clause under which action should be taken. Mr. Leach and himself had visited the cottages, and found tuere was not sufficient land to carry out the improvements. The burden of providing requisite accmunodation, he thought, should be thrown upon the owner.—Mr. Lake said the recommendation should be altered, so that it would read that in non- compliance with the notice served the property would be closed.—This suggestion was accepted, and the minu- tes were adopted.

div.head: FINANCE COMMITTEE.
div.p: FINANCE COMMITTEE.

The Finance Committee proposed that Joshua Nall assist the collector in collecting the general district rate and the water rate and that he be guaranteed in tile sum of £lOO ; also that the market superintendent write out the rate receipt books for the above-named rates and that his salary be increased £lO a year in consideration of such extra work. In proposing the adoption of the minutes and the finan- cial statement, Mr. Lightburn remarked that since the issue of the agenda paper the committee had decided, to invest £3OO of water sinking funds in the .Corporation of St. Helens for the next seven years at 3- per cent.— In reply to Mr. Bisbrown he thought the alteration in the staff mentioned would be sufficient. The treasurer's balances showed the overdrafts to be very large. They were charged at a high rate of interest on this, and the appointment of Nall was to reduce this and thus cause a less expenditure on interest.—Mr. Bisbrown said that after the waterworks were taken over the duties of, the officials were revised and one collector was recommended • to get in the water and improvemen,-, rates. The result proved a disappointment as it was shown that one person could not do the work. He was as much as ever op- posed to the increase. and not wishing to ha illogical he was anxious to make that explanation. They were bound to provide assistance for Mr. Jories or they would have very great arrears. The present time was inoppor- tune for increasing salaries thought under the circum-• tarice4 he could not oppose the recommendation,— Mr. Speakman thought the recommendation was very, ' clear and did not know that any bet ter course could have been taken.—After some discussion ' Mr. Lightburn explained that Mr. Nall had hitherto as- sisted the collector by reminding people that their rates had not been paid and then Mr. Jones called for the money before taking proceedings. The proposed change would unable Nall to take receipts with him and receive the money as well as Mr. Jones. Respecting Mr. Gar- ret, market superintendent, he would have to do extra work and therefore should receive extra remuneration. —The minutes were eventuahly adopted.

THE PUBLIC LATHS QUESTION. Mr. Lake produced a request from Mr. Walter Collier for the following resolution to ho put upon the agenda ' paper for the next meeting :—" That this Board carry out the proposal embodied in the resolution passed at a meeting of ratepayers held on the 18th day of April, 1894, with reeard to the provision of public baths, and for- warded to the chairman of the Thiard." Toe ratepayers meetin., was held in the Public Hall, Runcorn, and the resolution which was passed by a large majority ran . as knows :—" That this meeting of ratepayers Icing convinced that public baths are necessary for Runcorn, urge the Runcorn Improvement Com- missioners to take the necessary steps for their provision." Mr. Collier had also informed him of his intention to move the first resolution at the next meeting of the Commissioners.—Mr. W. Collier said that at the last Board meeting he was told that a public meeting should be called so that ratepayers could express their opinion on the subject. Mr. Taylor was the chairman at that meeting and he knew the feel- ing expressed. It was one of the largest ever held in j the town. When the Commissioners bought the. Water-1 works at a cost of £70,000 there was a far less representa- tion of ratepayers and he hoped the Commissioners would take the meeting as a fair index of the feeling in favour of public baths. He trusted the Commissioners , would carry out the desire of the ratepayers and had pleasure in moving the resolution mentioned first.—Mr. T. Lea seconded.—Mr. Grice understood that a baths committee still existed and suggested that the matter be referred to them.—Mr. Handley proposed that the terms of the motion be altered to the effect that the 13,-,ard remit to the consideration of the baths committee the proposal embodied in the resolution submitted by • Mr. C;illier. It had been said that a great deal of in- formation was at the disposal of the committee and it . would be as well to look at this, before they proceeded further. He sympathised with Mr. Collier in the matter and thought that by the committee dealing with , the question they might draw up a satisfactory scheme that would commend itself to both sections. He thought it was - only reasonable j that Mr. Collier should adopt this course.—Mr. Collier j asked that before the matter was referred to the Com- mittee, the Board adopt the principle that baths were a necessity. The committee would then have something to work upon.—The Chairman Laid that as a member of the Board he would not pledge himself to anything. If the subject was referred to the committee it would be carefully considered and some proposal might be brought before the Board.—Mr. Grico said if they did decide to have baths he hoped they would be good ones and a credit to the -town.—Mr. Handley then moved his amendment.—Mr. E. Liaison seconded, and after being supported by several gentlemen, Mr. Collier fell in with it as also did his seconder, Mr. Lea.—The amendment was put to the meetine: and carried:
THE PROPOSIM OR WING DOCK FOR RUNCORN.

Letters were read from the Associated Shipwrights. Sot%.iety. Runcorn, and Mesirs. John Stubbs and Sons. Runcorn, petitionin.g the Commissioners to press the Ship Canal Company to carry out their original promise to construct a graving dock, or slip ways, &a. .The communications pointed out that under existing circum— stances there was no place in Runcorn available to repair vessels and consequently they had to go elsewhere. This proved a serious loss to the town.—Mr. Pritchard, as chairman of the committee, who had this matter in hand, proposed that the communications be referred to the General Purposes Ccimmittee who were fully awaro ' of the importance Af the subject and would give it their . due consideration.—Mr. 13isbrown in seconding said he ' thought the letters were from important quarters in the town. He understood that the Law Clerk was already corresponding with the Ship Canal Company, and lie honed the subject would receive the attention it 64,served. —The proposition was carried.

MARRIAGE OF MR. WALTER, TIMMINS
OF RUNCORN.

An event in which considerable interest was evinced was the marriage of Mr. Walter Timmins, C.E., of Trinits House, 'Halton-road, to Miss Ellen Isherwood, of Stanley Villas, Green way-road. The ceremony took place on Monday morning at Holy Trinity Church, Runcurn, the Rev. Dr. Preston officiating. A rather numerous congregation had as- sembled in the church when the wedding, party arrived. The bride was attired in a travelling costume of grey cloth, and carried a beautatul bouquet of flowers. She was accompanied by one bridesmaid, namely, Miss Head, and was given away at the altar by Mr. Wood, of Manchester. The bridegroom was attended by Mr. Frank Timmins (brother) as best man. Subsequent to the ceremony, and as the wedding party were leaving the sacred edifice, Mr. A. Savage ,killfutly played the Wedding March on the organ. Mr. and Mrs. Timmins left Runcorn by the 12.25 p.m. train for London, from whence they proceeded to Paris. In the afternoon an " At Home" was held at the bride's residence, Stanley Villas, where a large number of guests were entertained. A numerous list of valuable presents has been received

div.head: HEALTH OF RUNCORN.
div.p: THE HEALTH OF RUNCORN.
MEDICAL OFFICERS ANNUAL REPORT.

The annual report of Dr. McDougall, medical officer of health for Runcorn. has just been issued. It shows that during the year ending December last the number of cases of preventable diseases notified was the large number of 546, as compared with 272 the preceding year. The number of notification papers received was 554. In cotaparing these returns with those of the previous year, 144 were eases of smallpox compared whh 7 for 1692. Seventy-eight were cases of scarlatina compared with 45 during- 1892. Thirty-six were cases of diphtheria compared a ith 30. One was a case of membraneous croup compared with 3. Eighty- two cases were notified of typhoid lever as against 65 in the preceding year, and 142 cases (4 continued fever, compared with 78, 7 were cases of puerperal fever comp +red with 6. Only one ca,c of ty pints occurred campared with the same number in 1892. Fiity-five cases of erysipelas were notified compared with 34 in 1592. Tha total number of deaths registered within the Authority's sanitary district during the year amounted to 513, compared with 441 in 1892. 01 these deaths 187 were in children one year and under. Sixty-eight were our one and under five years. Seventeen were over five and under fifteen years. Thirty-one were fifteen and under twenty-five years. Oae hundred +Ltd thirty-nine were twenty-five and under sixty-live years, and 71 were sixty-five and upwards. Tile Lutal number of cl,?aths, viz., 513, represents a death rate of 256 per thousand or the estimated population, and it the 31 in- quest cases be deducted, the (teach ra-ie is thereby re- duced to 24.1 per thousand, as compared with 22 for Lhe total death rate, and 207 fur that, exAusive of inquest cases, in 1892. After having dealt with the various forms which disease took in Runcorn during the past year, and the measures adopt,ai to prevent tie spread, Dr. MeDouttall goes on to say that ta., aathuricy was well aware that for ti:e last four or rive eats, eliteric liver had been more or less prevalent at ee.-tiu.. peridds of the year, and would recognise the importance of adopting every means for improving the sanitation of the town, which was the most satisfactory method of com- bating these yearly recurrences.

div.head: TEM kDUCATION OF DULLARD.
div.p: TEM kDUCATION OF DULLARD.

The Clerk reported the receipt or the following letter —Education Department, 16. h April, 1894.—Adverting to your letter dated the 17iii eltimo I am directed to refer you to paragraph 5 of the Revised Instructions for the view taken by the Department of the Question which you raise as to the admission to an infant school or class of a child above the usual age of infants, whose previous education has been neglected. lam to add that boys over eight years must not be admitted to an infant school unless the office arrange:in-tits are suitable for a mixed school. As regards the refusal of the admission of Thomas Done, aged 10, at the Holy Trinity Boys' School, I am directed to say that if this was based only on the ground that the boy was ignorant, iny lords no not consider such refusal to have been reasonable. (See al tide 78 of the Code.) Their lordships consider that he is too old for an Infant School. A copy of this letter will be sent to the managers of the Holy Trinity Boys' School.—J. W. J. Stephenson—in reply to Mr. Taylor the Clerk said that since the receipt of the letter he had informed the mother of the boy that she must send her son to school. He did not know what had been done, but would find out during the week. If the boy was not going to school the mother would be nrought belore the Attendance Committee next week. THE GUARDIANS AND THE SCHOOL ENQUIRY OFFICER. Mr. Moss produced a letter from the Local Government Board to Mr. Bowyer referring to the latter's post as school enquiry officer. They concurred with the Guar- dians in the opinion that it was inexpedient that he should retain that position. They, however, before ac- ceding to the application of the Guariliatis,gave him an opportunity of voluntarily resigning the post,—Reolying to Dr. McDouga,ll,the Clerk said Mr. Bowyer had written saying that he would retain the office until he was re- moved by the Guardians.—Dr. McDougall thought that the Department did not recognise the fact that parents should apply to the relieving officer for fees for their children. They would not be wnliin, he thought, to pauperise the class for which the Education Act was • specially devised.. Mr. Bowyer had neen appointed to meet the difficulty, and he was glad that he had not voluntarily resigned. in removing him the Guardians and the Local Government Board would have to bear the odium.—Mr. Taylor asked if the Guardians had the power to enforce the resignation now.—The Clerk said it was not necessary for the Guardians to apply to the Education Department to enforce the resignation.—The Chairman upheld. Mr. Bowyer's action in the matter.— Mr. Taylor expressed surprise at the decision of the Local Government Board after the matter had beert explained to them.—Canon Wood inquired if the Educa- tion Department could be asked to approach the Local Government Board.—The Clerk thought it would prove fruitlrss.—The Chairman thought they could go no fur- ther in the matter now that it had been laid before Government.—Canon Wood asked if a question could not be raised in Parliament. The law was if parent& wished their fees paid in any particular school they had the right.to have them paid. He thought it was not very fair acting for any public body like the Guar- dians to put difficulties in the way of parents for the. sake of small suins.—Dr. McDougall considered that the intention of the Guardians was to get parents t) go to the relieving officer, but the intention of the Act was to avoid it,—The Chairman thought there was a great ob- jection on the part of parents in ma king application for fees to the relieving oaten—Dr. McDougall was of the opinion that the question could be very properly raised in the House of Commrins.—The Clerk intimated that having all the correspondence at hand he could draw up the case very simply.—Dr. McDougall thought that the ostensible objection of the Guardians was that Mr. Bowyer would not go to the workhouse. The fees were paid out of the local rates of the town, but the sal try of £5 for the officer Ca me nut of the union rate.—The Chairman said the matter was a mutual i,c,reernorit be- tween the School 110a.r4 and the Gaardian4 o relieve the difficulty experienced for some years in Letting, the chil- dren of poor parents to atieud school, who I loclared they would not go to the relieving offi:..er because it pauper- ised them. 'This was why Mr. Bowyer was appointed inquiry officer.—Canon Wood proposed that the Clerk be instructed to draw up is complete statement of the case for the purpose of its introduction into Parliament —The motion was „seconded by Dr. Gastaldi wino re- marked that the G ardians cont‘nded that they were spending more on the salary than they were in fees.— The Clerk said unfortunately that was not so now as the distress in the town had increased tke fees.—The pro- position was carried after which the proceedings terminated.

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.

" BLESSED ARS Tilt PEACEMAItERS." GeorYe. Lewis, 1, Kent-st., was summoned at the war- rington'Borough Court on Friday, at the instance of his wife Mary Ann Lewis for assaulting her on April 21st. The case was a melancholy one, showing that the two parties had not lived comfortably together for some time. The magistrates decided to adjourn the case for one month to see if the parties could come to terms. As the &fend- ant was going out of the dock, Mr. Hunt, the chief con- stable, noticed a Ihtte girl near Mrs. Lewis. He askAl the defendant whether that was his daughter, to which defendant replied that she was. " Well then no to your wife, shake hands, and be friends," said Mr. Hunt. l'he defendant at once went to his wife, offered his hand, which she took, and they and their daughter went out of the court together, with Alderman Harrison's parting blessing of " Blessed are the peacennliers " sounding in their ears.

STRANGE COND7CT OF A WARFI.INGTON BARRER. John Stocks, a ha,rber in the Msrkt Plac, was brought before the Warrington magistrates on Monday, charged with hehlg apparontly of unsound mind, found wanclerin, at large in l'riestky-st., on April The Chi-f C, oo•t t Nesaid that the defertdant was a liairdreascr and had hved for many years in Warrington. Som!- time ago Le lost his wife, and bPaame very mach depresied in cr,nsegoehee. On April 19, he left his home and nothing was heard of him until two o'clock on the after- noon fth • 21st,when P.C.F•l'stia met him, in Priestlos- st. ie wns acting in a strange manner, and was bleed- ing troil As 11,:i did not; appi-ar rssponsible for his a he was brought to the police statlon,and Mr. Aukland, relieving officer, took him to the hospital, where he remained until that morning. The defendant had been discharged as being all right. When he . was brought to the police station a razor was found upon him, but the wound in the neck was not very deep.—ln reply to the magistrates, the defendant said that he thought he was all right, and that he thought he could take Carp rf himself, The magistrates therefore

RoWDY WOMEN IN THE COURT. I.l4a.rgaret Flannagan, and Kate Gerrard, both of Hop- wood-St., were each charged with being drunk and die- orderly in Hopwood-st., on April 23rd. P.C. Berry proved the cases. Flannigan stated chat some otheT women in Hopwood-st., had a spite against her becduse they thought she had " rounded "upon them for keep- ing a gambling club. Kate Gerrard said that the other women were pitching into her because she ate beef on a Friday. She thanked God that she had money to buy beef at all, and she would eat it on a FridAy in spite of anyone. She was not a "Roman Catholic Protestant." Several witnesses were called in support of thecharge of drunkenness and there then ensued a repititicn of the scene in Hopwood-st. The women commenced shouting at each other, and bra time the police officers found it impossible to stem the torrent of abuse coming foiss both witnesses and defendants.—When peace was at length restored the magistrates fined each defendant ss. and costs, and hoped that Mr. Hunt would inquire whether there was any truth in Flannagan's statement about the gambling club. ALLEGED ILLTREATMENT OF A HORSE. Mr. John Maginn,of the firm of Magian Bros—Sankey- st., was summoned at the Warrington Borough Court, on Friday, before Alderman Harrison, Alderman Wright, and Mr. J. H. Fleming, on the charge of cruelly illtreat• in, a horse by beating and kicking the same, on April 167 Henry Thornton said that on the above date he was coming from Bank Quay Station along Museum-street. When he entered the street he saw the defendant abus- ing the horse fearfully for some time. He was thrashing it with the whip, and he kicked it in the stomach very heavily with the toe of his shoe, three or four different times. He also thrashed it so much that he broke the whip. He also had a rope three or four yards long which was fastened to the bit of the horse, and he kept pulline, at the rope while the horse kept backing. After he had broken the whip he got two other whips to use upon the, horse. Witness then went for an officer, who came up, and after he had warned defendant, he desisted. Wit- ness was watching the affair for twenty minutes. He remonstrated with the defendant before he went for the ' officer.—James Beamont Clare gave corroborative evi-1 dence.l,lln cross-examination witness admitted the horse was "jibbing," and that defendant efferecl £2O for any one to take the horse into a field.—P.C. Corcoran, Ssrgt. , Cheney, and Inspector Spinks each gave evidence to seeing whip marks upon the horse's shoulders, but none of them saw any marks of kicking upon the lower parts of the body.—lnspector Luff said that defendant camel to him on Wednesday and admitted thrashing the horse. —The defendant said that he admitted beating the horse because he had to beat it, but he perhaps would not have beaten it so much if he had been let alone. In the esent case he was doing the best he could for the horse, and did nothing to the horse to injure its health other- wise than was necessary to cure a " jibbing " horse. The horse had been sold to him and when he took it out he found it to be a" jibber," and rather than sell it and "take in,, someone else, he preferred to break It in. Since that night, it had given no trouble at all.— John Dixon, veterinary surgeon, said that he examined the horse the same night as the alleged beating, and found some marks upon the shouldors. There were no marks of kicking upon the body. The horse was in good condition, and as it was fleshy, it would not take a heavy lash to mark it.—Mr. John Flesketh, of Museum- street, said that he saw the whole occurrence. He did not think that the defendant did anything but what was necessary to cure a jibbing horse. He would have done the same himself. He never saw the defendant kick the horse at all, and he considered Mr. Thornton's interfer- ence uncalled for.—After consultation among the magis- trates, Alderman Harrison in giving their decision,made an admonitory address to the defendant concerning the treatment of hsrses,of almost ten minutes duration, and said that the magistrates had decided to fina him 20s. and costs.

;TUESDAY.—Before Mr. R. Garnett (chairman), and Dr.

Starkey Susita. DUNE. AND DISORDERLY.—James Leigh, an elderly man was charged on a warrant with being drunk and disorderly in Mersev-street on the 23rd int.t. P.C. Amson proved the case. He was fined 10g. and costi or 14 days' imprisonment. SEVERE SENTENCE ON A YOIITH.—James Roark, aged 20, was charged with being drank and disorderl_e in Rylands-street, the previous night. and further charged with assaulting Inspector Spinks, P.C. Barlow, and John Bibby and Joseph Potter at the same time and place. Margaret Roark, sister of the prisoner was charged with assaulting Inspector Sinks, and attempting to rescue the prisoner. From the evidence of Inspector Spinks it appesred that he was called to the Royal Court Theatre at 9.45 the previous night. When he arrived at the entrance he saw the prisoner assault Mr. Potter and Mr. Bibby. On the prisoner seeing him he ' rushed at him and kicked him on the hip. Inspector Spinks closed with him, and while they were on the floor the prisoner tried to bite him, and acted in a very violent manner. Ultimately the prisoner was taken to , the Public Hall Hate' where he broke a pane of glass and again assaulted the Inspector. Toe female defen- dant dragged at the Inspector's tunic, took his stick from him-, and several times tried to get the prisoner away. P.C. Barlow said he saw the prisoner kick Inspector Spinks in the lobby of the Public Hall Hotel. The prisoner kicked witness on the finger, and the female prisoner tried to get the prisoner fiom them. P.C. Amami gave evidence as to seeing the prisoner kick Inspector Spinks, and butt P.C. .Barlow in the head. The prisoner acted like a madman. Mr. Josepu Potter, of the Royal Court Theatre, stated that he heard a row taking place at the entrance to the theatre. He left his box and saw the prisoner quarrelling with the ticket collector. He asked the reason from the ticket collector and he told him that the prisoner had been disorderly, and he refused to give him a "check." The prisoner got hold of witness by the throat and threw him down. The Inspectar then came and took him into custody. Mr. Bibby, ticket collector, said at quarter past nine lie went to the prisoner and asked him to go out, as he had had several complaints as to his conduct. At the interval he refused to have him in the building, and the female defendant tried to persuade her brother to go home. He refused and afterward 3 assaulted Mr. Potter. The female defendant got hold of witaess by the coat collar, and also tore his tie and collar.—The defendant said he was drunk and did not know what he was doing, and the female defendant said she would not have inter- fered had not the Inspector struck him with a stick. The magistrates fined the female defendant 10s.or in default seven days' impriaonment,and the male prisoner was committed to gaol for two months. KICKING A Doon IN.—James Lynch was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Bridge-st., and further charged with doing wilful damage to a dof.r belonging to Mr. George Wheeler, 3, Coronation Buildings. P.C. Robinson stated that about g. 30 the previous night, he was at Market Gate in company with Constable! Lewis when a woman complained to him of the prisoner's drunkenness, and said he had kicked the panels of a door in. They went to the house where the prisoner lived, and found the panels of the door knocked in. Toe prisoner bad left but they found him drunk in Bridge-st. P.C. Lewis corroborated. Mr. Wheeler stated that he went home at 2.30 the previous afternoon, and the pris- oner was in the house. He attempted to throw at knife at his (witness's) wife, and also kicked him. He had to be put out, but soon afterwards he returned, and finding the door fastened he kicked the panels in. DAMAGING STREET LiMPS.—Two Lois [ARUM Robert Edwards, and JAMES Buckley, of Earleatown. were charged with having on the 10th April damaged a gas lamp belonging to the Newton Improvement Commis- sioners. Mr. J. E. Worsley, clerk to the Commissioners, prosecuted. He stated that the two defend ints had dome damage to a gas lamp to the extent of 33. The Newton Commissioners had for thelast two years suffered very seriously indeed by persons throwing stoneS at the gas lamps. They issued notices offering £2 reward to anyone who would give information as to the persons who did the damage. The lamplighter was also set to watch,and he succeeded in catcking the two boys throw- ing stones at a lamp, and damaging it. They were ! liable for such an offence to a penalty not exceeding £5 in addition to the amount of damage done. There was no wish to unduly press the case, but it was brought forward with a view that the case might stop the boys in the di3trict from damaging the Commissioners' pro- perty.—Thomas Mellor, Lamplighter, said he saw the two defendants damaging a lamp a little before tan ! o'clock on the night of the date named. Two panes af glass were broken, and had there been any wind the light would have been blown out. Within a short space of time they had had as many as 40 or 50 lansps brolv.l3, and had been unable to account far it. The magistrates fined the defendants 53. each including costs, and the Chairman remarked that if any similar cases came before them they woald be dealt with much more severely. div.head: WAI-:EINGTON v. ST. HELENS HECTEATION.
div.p: WAI-:EINGTON v. ST. HELENS HECTEATION.

The Bughv football season came to a conclusion on Saturday, ..vlien for the third time this seasian the home premier team. encountered St. Helens Recreation. On one of the previous eccasions, Warrington issued from the match victorious, whilst on the other occasion a draw was the result. The visitors placed a good team on the field on Saturday, and a victory was anticipated by their supporters. . Their anticipations, however, were not thinned. Although the Wirepullers were with- out the services of Jolley, Nevins, and Carey, they showed some excellent form and finally secured a credit- able victou. The teams were of the following composi- tion :

Warrington : Boscow, back; Massey, Evans, Potts, and Heesom, three-quarters; James Bate and John Bate, half-backs ; Turner, Taylor, Dakin, Berry, Thorniley, Houghton, Buckley, and Bailey, forwards. st. Helens Recreation : Ponnineten, back ; Hughes, *Prow, Seddon, and Sidler, tree-quarters; Harper and Molyneux, half- hacks; Mouadaie, Fildes, Briers, Donnelly, Yates, Houghton, Chapman, and Mercer, forwards. Turner started towards the pavilion goal, and the game opened in a somewhat senational manner. After Boseow and Seddon had exchanged kicks the Warrington forwards screwed the first scrimmage in clever style, and John Bate fielding well when the oval became loose, a pass tio Evans siNV that player executing a clinking run in from half way, loud cheers greeting the clever performance. No goal resulted from Turner's attempt. Evans met the drop out, arid the locals came very near scoring an:tin through the instrumentality of Taylor. Seddon defended well, and kicking judiciously a local had a kick charged so that the home goal was placed in jeo- pardy. The defence was equal to the attack, and Da kin eventually led the way past the hall line, but the locals being penahz-d. Seddon again gave his side a footing near the pavilion goal with a ponderous punt. James Bate kicked smartly from behind a scrimmage, and quick following up saw Pennington floored, whilst a moment later James Bite got finely away. hut his pass to Taylor was a shade too high, and a capital opening was thus lost. Ilouehton, Berry and Turner further improved Warrington's position, but a round of passing by the home backa was upset by Seddon, who cleared the locals out to half way. The home forwards continued to hold the upper hand, and after Massey and Heesom had dis- tinguished themselves;Daltin, Thorniley and Bailey each in turn led the forwards, only to see Pennington accom- plish some smart saves. Another good bit of passing by Melyneux,-Harper, Trow and Seddon saw the latter effecting another fine run, but Boscow could not he passed, whilst the lost ground was speedily regained when the Warrindton custodian found touch at the Rec,'s. quarter flag. Pones and Evans each in turn tried hard to get throueh with ill success, and exchanges between Trow, Brown,and Pennington resulted in the last named muffins, and the Faints' goal narrowly escaping disaster. Heesom made a bold bid on the popular side, but was . cared for by Hughes, whilt a smart dash by Berry nearly eadn'd n something tangible. Thrice over James Bate Was apnlauded fur esvar marks, and though Sed- don and Trevor got the oval out of danger,Boaeow could not be.p,assed and the game rarely escaped the visitors' quarters. Toorniley next took an opening in line style, but he preferred to pass to a comrade and the chance was missed, whilst another was presented when Penn- ington mulled an accurate return lay Hassey. Sidier next dribbled well for the Saints and the Warrington quarters were invaded', and •in response James and John Bate, Berry and Dakin dribbled past half way, and the inter- val arrived with Warrington leading' by a try to nil. Like the preceding half, the concluding half opened in a somewhat sensational manner. After Heesom had been applauded for some clever kicking in reply to Seddon and Trowna•last dribble executed by Houghton saw the oval worked over the coveted line, and this promising forward completed a piece of work, which Potts suc- ceeded in augmenting from a difEcnit position. Taylor an Turner led the way to the 8:. Helens line asrain,and Peanineton again had his hands full. Mausdale and Fildes relieved alightAr, and then came a passing move- ment started by the Bat es, Potts knoeking on in the final esaan'.., Therniley and Berry rushed the leather to the line oni7 to meet with a stubborn defence, and the lengthencel attack ended in Pennington conceding another alinoin Turner was to the fore with a good run soon after tire drop out, and when it lo,.;ked long odds on the le to :heir saere ova,: aaxiety saw them pen. and ;,A1 -u's kick found touch at half way. FA.rs was tice c.tul?ued far foul work, whilst Dakin got .finely away from a line out, and faulty field- ing by the local backs spoilen an easy chance of scoring. Minors fell to the credit of Warrington in quick sue- zeesion, and lieesom was held a yard inside after a des- perate effort. File game raged cniefly in the St. Helens (le:liners alter this, and after several efforts, Evans dribbled prettily through the thick of his opponents,and managed to steer the oval over the line, but when in the act of grounding he lost possession and a minor was all that was rnorcigl. Final :—Warrington, one goal one try ; St Helens Recreation, nil.

WeeeliedeoN V. ST. HELENS RECREATION " A " TEABI9. A small " gate "assembled at the St. Helens Recreation encioeure on Saturday, when these teams met. The teams were scarcely representative, for in the Warring- ton combination several juniors appeared and all ac- quitted themselves creditably. St. Helens kicked off, and a quick response being forthcoming from Clark, the vieitora were early aggressive. Clark was again pro- minent, and another effort of his almost brought about tha downfal) of the Saints' goal. A free kick to the home side relieved slightly, but Warrington would not be denied the attack, and clever play by the front rank gave the home custodian trouble. Again did the Saints respond, and by way of a change the Warringtonians were placed on the defensive. A free kick gave welcome relief, and Gibson effecting a good run spoiled the effort by dallying with his pass. A minor eventually accrued to the visitors, and although free kicks were granted in quick succession to the home side, the Warrington for- wards maintained their superiority and rarely allowed he Saints to escape their quarters, Fairhurst and Knight d'esplaying good form. Randles had a rare chance, but a pass forward spoiled the opening, whilst Thornton took a drop at goal, the shot going wide of the desired mark. Fortune, however, favoured the aggres- sors a few minutes later, for the Warrington skipper securing possession literally forced his way over, and Fester gave his side a substantial lead by placing a neat goal. Chapman and Moores showed up after the re- start with judicious kicking, and after a spell of even play, Tayler got over for the • locals and placed the sides on an equal footing by kicking a goal. The Rees' suc- cess stimulated the vieitors to renewed exertion, and. Foster got in, but the point was overruled, and the in- terval arrived with each side having a goal to their credit. Resuming, Warrington early showed up, anci Moores displayed his sterling worth by scoring a clever try, which Gibson failed to convert. The Warrington forwards continued to allow the home side no quarter, and after Fairhurst, Lawless, and Clark had displayed rood form, Holmes dribbled well, whilst a fine run by Ladle locked finish. The Recs, had a brief look in at the Warrington quarters, hut Clark got the sphere out of danger, and after being slightly damaged, succeeded in scoring from a scrimmage, Foster again doing the need- ful. Near the close the home team took advantage of a misundersta.nding of the visitors, and the outcome of the error was a try to Taylor, which was not improved up- on, and a good game ended in a win for the Warring- tonians by two goals and a try to St. Helens Recreation a goal and a try. RuNcome A" V. BIRKENHEAD WANDERERS: LIVER- POOL RUGBY LEAGUE.—This fixture was played off on Saturday afternoon at St. Anne's enclosure, Birkenhead, before a fair number of spectators. The Runcorniane started and for some time very even play was witnessed. At length the visitors placed the opposiag team on the defensive, and Snaps was tackled on the line whilst endeavouring to clear. Heavy scrimmaging ensued near to the St. Anne's citadel, but all efforts at scoring were futile. Play now moved towards the visitors' territory and after some nice dribbling by Atkinson, Webb was enabled to score the first and only try for thb Birkenhead men. The attempt at goal failed. This success on the part of their opponents seemed to put new life into the Runcornians who immediately began to press, and fol- lowing some hard tactics, equalized, before the call of half-time. In the second half of the encounter both organizations tried their utmost to improve their respeo- tiee scares but could not succeed, the game thus ending in a draw of one try each. RUNCORN V. BROUGHAM—These teams tried conclu- sions on Saturday afternoon before about 2,000 specta- tersem the Irwell-lane enclosure, Runcorn. Operations were commenced by W. Faulkner, and after a bit of smart play the homesters invaded the visitors' territory where a scrimmage easued. The Broughton men even- tually broke away, but were stopped in mid-field. Run- corn now began again to press, and after a neat bit of passing Richardson scored amidst enthusiastic shooting. The attempt at goal was given to Butterworth, who failed "to bring it off." The homesters continued to press their opponents and added another try before half time, when the score stood : Runcorn, 2 tries; Brough- ton,nothing. Upon resuming play Broughton went away with a dash, hut were soon sent to;the right-about, and for the remainder of the game had to play second fiddle. Some beautiful passing was seen on the part of the home team, who had all the bast of the play. Two tries were added by Morris and Abrams, and at the call of full time, Ruacorn were the victors by 4 tries to nil.

div.head: JUNIOR RUGBY CUP COMPETITION.
div.p: THE JUNIOR RUGBY CUP COMPETITION.
ST. MARY'S v. LATCRFORD. _ UNDECIDED FINAL TIE.

The final tie—or what should have been the final tie— of the above competition was played on Monday night, on the Warrington football ground, before a" gate "of abcut 4,000. • The cup and medals, which were to be presented to the winners at the close of the game, were on view on the grand stand,. and were very much ad- mired. A neutral referee in the persan of Mr. J. Smith of Widnes officiated, and the game was begun, by Master Davies, son of Mr. P. Davies, the donor of the cup and m,dils, kicking off for Latchford. Latchford pressed considerably at the start, but Burton by one of his huge kicks caused them to assume the defensive,and Smith stopped a dangerous rush of St. Mary's, and by a good kick restored play to half way. Raybold however broke away, and Chapman only just saved a try. Im- mediately afterwards, a splendid round of passing be- tween the whole of the St Mary's three quarters, ended in Flampson being pulled up almost on the line. Carter for Latchford, however, restored considerable lost ground, but Hampson repelled the Latchford men by a long kick when embraced by an opponent. Raybold then made his mark at the half way line, and Burton made a good shot at goal, arill a minor however result- ing. After the kick out Raybold took a free kick which took play near the line, and Burton's attempt to drop a goal was charged down by Smith who made a good run through the opposing forwards to half way, where Roughley grassed him. Exchanges between Roughley and Chapman, saw the latter making almost his only mistake in the match, for being too slow with the ball, and a scrimmage ensued on the Latchford line. Hough- ton cleared well, but Sanders by kicking too hard caused a second minor to be conceded to the Saints. Soon after an attempt at drop goal by Raybold ended in , another minor for the Saints. After the restart Hughes ' ran along the touch line to near the line, but his career was stopped by Ray bold,whose return was very poor and almost let Latchford in. St. Mary's again returned to the attack, and a fourth minor fell to their lot. After a spell of monotonous scrimmages near half way, Burton made a splendid run, and when pressed, he kicked over his opponents' heads. Raybold rushing up ran almost to the line, when he was tackled by Chapman. He passed just at the right moment to Warburton, who with no one to stop him scored a try amid loud cheers from the St. Mary's supporters. Burton increased the try to five points. Half time immediately afterwards arrived with St. Mary'S leading by one goal to nil. The second half opened in a sensational manner, for after the usual ex- changes, Dakin dribbled through the thick of his oppo- nents, and then kicked from the 25 flag over the line where the ball came to a standstill. A race now ensued between Burton and Lord for possesion. Burton arrived first, but in his anxiety to kick dead, he simply grazed the top of the ball,and Lord coming just behind., dropped upon it, scoring a very lucky try. Carter made the scores equal by placing a goal. Each side now tried hard to gain a winning point, and exciting play ensued. Bennett spoiled a good run by a wild pass, al- though Burton was near with practically a free course before him. Dakin at this point was playing his best for Latchford, and it was principally his play which gave his side the supremacy during this part of the game. For about ten minutes there was a succession of scrimmages within ten yards of the St. Mary's line, and Latchford was decidedly unlucky, when at length Bur- ton got the ball loose, and put his side on the offensive again. Latchford however returned to the attack, and Roughley only just saved in time by canceding a minor. In spite of all the exertions of the teams, neither could score, and full time arrived with the score of a goal each. It was now decided to play twenty minutes extra time— ten minutes either way. Latchford kicked off, and St. Mary's fora time held the upper hand, but Latchford qiiickly recovered, and Roughley made such a bad at- tempt to save that it almost cost his side a try. Burton had another drop at goal, but was again unsuccessful, only gaining a barren minor. The same player soon afterwards took a free kick which was charged down, and caused the St. Mary's team considerable anxiety. St. Mary's after this fright recovered their lost ground, and Warburton got over the line, but the point was not allowed to the evident disappointment of the " Marys," owing to the player being slightly off side. The first ten minutes now expired with no alteration to the score. In the second " ten "Warburton again almost got over, but was pulled up by a Latchford player, who owing to the increasing darkness could not be distinguished. This portion of the game arrived with the scores still equal. Alter consultation it was decided to play two five minutes extra time again, and the tired out players again toed the line. It was now almost dark, and the players could scarcely be distinguished, but from all ap- pearances they were very equally matched. Suffice it tie say when the extra time was finished, neither side had gained an extra point, and the game was again drawn. It was now too dark to play any more. The cup and medals had been announced to be presented upon the field to the winners of the game, but as neither team could beat'the other, this ceremony could not be per- formed, and Mr. Warren had to take possession of it again,

div.head: ALLEGED BIGAMY AT RUNCORN.
div.p: ALLEGED BIGAMY AT RUNCORN.
OVER WITH THE CAPTAIN AND ON .WITH
THE MATE.

A case of bigamy, possessing no little amount of interest and productive of some amusement was heard by Mr. F. J. Norman on Friday (last week) at the Runcorn Police Court.—Mary Dagnall, twenty-six years of age, was charged with having feloniously married Jesse Duckers on the 9th April at the Runcorn Parish Church, her former husband being then alive. Jesse Dockers, twenty-nine years of age, was also charged with having aided and abetted Mary Dagnall in the commission of the offence.—Esther Massey, 75, Nelson-st., deposed to being present at the Runcorn Parish Church when William Dagnall was mar- ried to the female prisoner on the 26th May, 1885. ShQ signed the register as witness.—Matilda Withey, 13 a Egerton-st., said that for the six weeks during which she had known the female prisoner, the latter had gone , under the name of Mary Beckett. She witnessed the marriage on April 9th at the Parish Church, and heard Mary Dagnall answer "No" when asked by the Rev. J. Holden if she had been previously married.—James Hig- gins, employed by Messrs. Simpson and Davies as fore- man, testified to Mr. and Mrs. Dagnall haying had charge of two narrow boats for some years. The man Dockers had acted as mate to William Dagnall on one of the boats. Dagnall had lived with his wife up to about eighteen months age—Margaret Ralph asserted that she had seen Duckers haying tea with* Mr. and Mrs. Dagnall several times. He knew that they were mar- ried, having, on one occasion, seen the marriage certifi- cate. Packers had remarked to witness that he would not carry such a wiman as Mrs. Dagnall on a boat with Dagnall, the original husband of the female prisoner, stated that he was engaged on the nar- row boat "Friend," and resided in High-st., Runcorn. He had known Duckers for about three years, he having sailed with witness as mate for some months on the boats "John" and "Emma." Duckers knew perfectly well that he (witness) and the female, Mary Dagnall, were married.--Inspector Cooper produced two certifi- cates of marriage. One of them showed that William Dagnall was married to Mary Beckett (maiden name of female prisoner) on the 26th May, 1885; the second showed that Jesse Puckers was married to Mary Beckett, spinster, on the 9th April, 1894. The first marriage ceremony was performed by the Rev. Robert Edwards and the second by the Rev. J. Holden. Continuing, Inspector Cooper said that he had examined the certifi- cates with the register of marriages at the Parish Church, and found them to be correct copies. He apprehended both prisoners in Bridge-st., Runcorn, at 11.30 on the night of the 23rd April. When the charge was read over to them at th. police station the female replied that she knew her husband was alive but he had married her under a wrong name. The male prisoner said that Mary Dagnall had told him that she was not lawfully married to Dagnall he having gone through in a wrong name.—ln reply to the Deputy Magistrates' Clerk Mary Dagnall said that she had received a letter (produced) from the mother of Wm. Dagnall which stated that the real name of her (prisoner's) husband was" William Henry Sparrow." During the time which she (Mary Dagnall) had lived with her husband he had kicked, and otherwise ill-used her. He had dragged her down by the hair of her head to the cabin floor and threatened her if she dared to raise an alarm. He had crippled her right arm so that she could not do a hard day's work; and in fact he had se frightened her that she was afraid to remaia in the same cabin with him when night came on.—Duckers, in answer to the Clerk, pleaded that the female prisoner had told him that she was not lawfully married to Dagnall. He did not want to get married, bet she would have them married.—The prisoners were committed to take their trial at the next Chester Assizes, bail being granted upon two sureties being produced of £25 each, and another of £5O.

div.head: LITTLE RECRUIT.
div.p: A LITTLE RECRUIT.

Under existing laws, the French military authorities cast their nets tolerably wide for recruits, but the mesh, even now, must not be made too small. At Asniers, at what is called the Council of Revision, a conscript pre- sented himself the other day whose height was 73 centimetres, or about 2 feet q inches. This is about the height of an ordinary child two years of age,whereas the conscript was nineteen. Although it could not be alleged that he could claim exemption owing to physical infirmity of any kind, he was naturally excused from serving.

div.head: COAL TRADE.
div.p: THE COAL TRADE.
MASTERS WANT A REDUCTION OF WAGES.

At a meeting of coalowners hQld in Manchester on Tuesday the question:of a reduction in the rate of wages was considered. Prices of coal, it was said, were mire- munerative, and there was a general opinion that a "substantial reduction" in wages was necessary ; but no definite step was taken by the meeting. DEMAND FOR REDUCTION IN SCOTLAND. - -

The coalmasters of Ayrshire, of Lanarkshire, and of Airdrie and Slamannan have intimated a reduction of is. per day in miners' wages, The reduction has been reported to the Miners' Federation, whose advice will guide the miners in their attitude to the proposal.

GREAT DEPRESSION OF TRADE. The coal trade is depressed both in Yorkshire and Derbyshire. Nearly 1,000 miners are out of work in the Thorncliffe district, near Sheffield. On Wednesday the colliers employed in the Tankenloy pit held a meeting, and decided to ask the owners Messrs. Newton, Cham- bers, and Co., not to close the mine. In the event of the withdrawal of the notices the men promise to send a better quality of coal to the pit bank. At Little flulton, in this county, a colliery is being closed" in consequence of the extreme depression of trade."

"A GENEROUS CORPORMION."

house let at £2O a year; in five years it increased to £4O. 'hen I asserted that thk town was under-assessed I calcu- lated the per capita wealth at. £lOO. According to statistics published on the subjt.ct the per capita wealth at the present time is £250. div.head: MORE CRITICISMS AM) SUGGESTIONS.
div.p: MORE CRITICISMS AM) SUGGESTIONS.

The gentleman whose views we published last week but one on the subject of municipal finance, one day this week expressed his opinions to an " Examiner " reporter upon the criticisms by Coon- ' cillor J. Shaw Green which we published last week. " In the interview with Councillor J. Shaw Green which you published last week, I believe he stated that the scheme for widening the streets was more a pleasant dream than a possible reality." " I believe those were his words." "Some day it will be an actual reality. Warrington occupies a sinunlo.r position. She is situated exactly midway between London and Glasgow and midway between Manchester and Liverpool,four of the largest cities in Great Britain, She has at her door the Manchester Ship Canal. Which has recently converted her into a seaport. All the large railways. the L. & N.W., the Great Western, the Great Northern, the Midland, the Great Eastern, and the Manchester, Sheffield, and Lincolnshire are in direct communication with the town, besides which she will be in the near future the terminus of the Lancashire, Derbyshire, and East Coast Railway. With these extraordinary examples of commercial and engineering greatness, it seems difficult to realise how the Corporation of Warrington can allow the present system of high ways to exist any longer. Despite Mr. Green's views to the contrary I think energetic steps will sooner or later have to be aken to remedy the disadvantages of streets that have been in existence since the middle ages. In fact I believe the Corporation are purchasing property to carry this work out in piece-meal fashion." " Yes, / understand that is so." " If the Corporation are adopting that course, the better plan for them would be to get the work done at once and make one comprehensive scheme."

" Row would you propose to do this ?" "The Corporation should build a block of ten shops four stories high, in a convetient position and set hack to the full width of the proposed widened thoroughfare. When one block is completed, oper- ations should be started in demolishing the property in the streets that require actually widening. Ten shops at a time, might be demolished and the ten- ants allowed to inhabit the new shops already erected." _ _ _

" I suppose that misiderable objection would be raised to this. First because ot the inconvenience, and secondly because of the loss which shopkeepers would experience in ehifting their stand." "So far as the inconvenience is concerned the improvement is necessary and the disturbed ten- ants would have the option ot returning to their original site after the improvement was carried out with the certainty of improved trade by reason of the facilities created for business."

"There are buildings I suppose which are con- sidered to be in such a satisfactory state that the expense entailed in demolishing them would be seriously objected to." "in cases of this kind the buildings could be pushed back without being demolished and re- built. Ordinary buildings such as those in our town can by a certain engineering method be lifted in a bulk from their present foundations and placed on new foundations. I have seen this work done constantly and know that it is quite practicable and not very expensive." "This done you would of course consider the laying of cable roads practicable." " Decidedly. The system is good and in vogue in Birmingham, and other towns. I think it would be absurd to allow a private company to carry out the work as suggested by Mr. Green. The roads would have to be taken up and no one is better qualified to direct the operations than the town officials. The cable road ought to be run through the centre of the town in order that the public might be in immediate com- munication with the shops. It would neither pay the Corporation nor a private company to run a system of conveyances as Mr. Green suggested through the side greets. The opposition even of 'busses which would run in the main streets would be fatal." "Bat Mr. Green as you will see pointed out that the burdens at present pressing upon the town necessitate the postponement of such a large scheme as you have mentioned." " I have already pointed out that the burden im- posed alien the town is in the direction of the administration of her finance. It really does not matter whether the money is borrowed at four per cent and invested at 2:i per cent as I proved, or whether it is borrowed at 31 and invested at 3 as admitted by Mr. Green, the principle is bad. If you buy iron at ..C4 per ton and sell it at £3 per ton whether you be a nrivate individual or a corpora- tion, the process sooner or later is bound to laud you in difficulties." " But .Ntr. Green pointed out that there was only one solitary case where money was borrowed at 4 per cent interest and another where money was inveeted at 2.1 per cent." "The Borough Treasurer's accounts contain more than one instance. The Diocese of Manchester are paid 4 per cent for money borrowed whilst money received from the Bridgewater Trustees on account for Coal Royalty in invested at `..2 per cent." " You contend that money could he borrowed at less than 3zl: and 31 per cent as paid by the Warring- ton Corporation?' " Decidedly.. People would be glad to invest their money at 24 per cent in municipal stock. I have in my hand at present proof—which you may see— of a firm in Warrington investing over a quarter of a million at money at 2a per cent. Not- tingham 31.er cent Corporation stock was at 102 k per cent premium last week. This wilt show that the rate of interest paid by the Warring- ton Corporation is too high, and that the Finance Committee are altogether too generous with the re tepayere' money. It reminds me of an old story of two friends who slept together, one of whom Ott rising in the morning put on. his companions trouaere,and pulled out of the pocket half-a-crown, with which be "tipped ",the attendant. When his friend remarked upon his generosity, he discovered that they had exchanged trousers. The moral being, that it is very easy to be generous with another person's money.' " Did .you study Mr. Green's comments on your arguments for the consolidation of the debt ?" " Yes. Mr. Eileen's objection was that a large portion of the Borough debt had been taken up by way of annuities, and that difficulties would be en- countered in arranging terms with the owners of tbeee annuities. I contend that, the repayment of these annuities can eaeily be effected by Sp-cial Act of Parliament which obliges lenders to receive beck their principal in exactly the same way it obligee landoweere and property owners to sell land for puhlie undertakings.. So that this his chief ohjection talls`to the ground." " Did you read Mr. Green's ob,ervatitms an your proposal to procure a hill for the extent-lon of time for lomis that would he taken up when the debt was consolidated • "Yes. According to the interview, Mr. Green questioned my knowledge of the manner in which these things are arranged. I may state that I have had considerable experience. I have been before a committee of the flouee of Lords and the House of Coeomone for the purpose of obtaining one of theee Privat.e. Acts. With regard to the extension of time for the repayment of the money invested in the Water Works the Finance Cemmittee.eccording to Mr. Greeneippear to think they made a big fight. before the Commons Committee. The public of Warrington think they made a remarkably small one. If the Corporation had really considered the immense importance that, the ext ension of time woeld here been to the ratepayers of Warringtoa they would have taken care, with the precedents at their command, that enceeee should hare alt ended their efferte. Tery got absolutely nothing but what the general net confers. I believe that a sub- stantial Citse can be made out for Warrington, and if the riefit Parliament e'ry Counsel be einployed,the extent ion required can be secured. The circurn- staucee of Warrington'e present position, if put be- fore the Committee propel ly, ,would justify this. The fact is, if the Watrili,:lt on Corporal ion do not widen the to roots and reduce the rates they will wake en one day to Ire fact, that a new town has sprung up et Stock ten Heath, mid Warrington will be left. 11. the Wallington streets are net, widened when the Docks are opened aol probabi y Ihe East Coast Roil way, the tieffie irons these sources whien meet cross the town will be terribly congested in th main t heroughfe ree as t !iey now exist.. The sE,rvela ought therefore to be widened is soon as possible." div.head: NEW PUBLIC HALL FOR WARRINGTON.
div.p: THE NEW PUBLIC HALL FOR WARRINGTON.
DETAILS OF THE BUILDING.

The new Public Hall, which Mr. J. Charlton Parr is about to build for the town, is, we understand to be constructed on very elaborate lines, and when finished will 136 the most complete building in War- rington. The work, which is to be carried out by Mr. William Owen, architect, and Mr. Collin, builder, has already been csmmenced, and is to be completed in twelve months. As we mentioned last week the site chosen is on the open space in Palmyra Square, abutting on the Gymnasium, and the estimated cost of erecting the building is £5OOO. The building will consist of a large hall with a gallery. The hall will run parallel with the road, and will be 30 yards long and 16 yards wide, inclusive of a spacious platform. The main entrance will be off Palmyra Square. It will consist first of a . space covered by an awning, then the entrance hall. In- tervening between the latter and the main lail is a corridor, which runs entirely round the hall, and which is to he heated with hot water pipes. Branching off from the entrance hall there will he ladies and gentlemen's retiring rooms with lavatory. From the hall there will be four exits as well as the main entrance doors. The rear of the gallery will be 107 feet by 65 feet, including an organ chamber, and there will be two spacious side galleries. There will also be here on the right hand side another ladies' retiring room and lavatory, Besides the main gallery stairway there will be four or more crush stairs with exit doors. On the ground floor, at the rear of the building there will be an addi- tional entrance for perforniers,where there will also be dressing rooms and lavatories. Near by there will be, on the basement, a kitchen and heating chamber. The height of the building from the floor to the ceiling wi:l be abont 45 feet. Ventilation of a most modern character will be provided, and the ceilings and decorative work is to he I of a high class order. Generally speaking the in- terior of the building is expected to be of a highly finished character. Of the size of architecture which is to be adopted for the exterior of the work, we are unable at present to speak, although we understand the style is to be neither strikingly elaborate nor plain.
