div.head: WARRINGTON WRESTLER AT ST. HELENS.
div.p: A WARRINGTON WRESTLER AT ST. HELENS.
" FAIR " TURNER AND TOM CANNON.

At the People's Palace, St. Helens, on Friday night, "Fair" Turner the well-known athlete and footballer, ot Warrington, met Tom Cannon in a wrestling match in the Geteee-roman Style. The champion had offered £lO to anyone whom he failed to put down in fifteen minutes. A very spirited encounter was the result of the contest, and when time was nearly up, Cannon managed to get his opponent in a favourable position on the ground and secured a fall ;, but Fair Turner was off the canvas and the referee and timekeeper kMr. J. T. Fletcher) did not award the match to Cannon. Both wrestlers then agreed to continue for anothee fifteun minutes, and when twelve minutes had passed Cannon was again in the better position: It was then &Paled that the champion got hold of Turns r' leg, which in that particular style of wrestling constitutes a foul, and Mt. Fletcher gave a foul against Caenon ; but as the match was not for a wager he was not adjudged the 15,ser. The contestants were too fatigued for anether fifteen minutes' bout, and it was agreed that Tureer shou:d meet Cannon again on SAturday night. Before the final arrangements were made Cannon stated to the audience that he would lay £lOO to £2O that he would beat Turner in the next match. This'cballenge was not, however, accepted. There was again a large house on Saturday evening, and Turner was again accordod a hearty reception. The contestants soon got to work, and though the Warrine- t onian acted mainly on the defensive, there were OCC3- sions when he adopted the ag,gressive, and had his more experienced opponent in difficult positions. However, after more than ten minutes' work. Cannon assumed the upper hand,arid gradually forcing his opponent by sheer strength and weight succeeded in throwing the amateur lafter twelve moautes' wrestling. Loud cheers greeted both men at the close, and the Warringtonian was com- plimented on all sidas for the plucky stand he had made.

div.head: iitttero to the 450ttor.
div.p: iitttero to the 450ttor.
THE SOCIAL PANACEA.

" The horse-leech's daughter still crying for more." Sir,—Your Socialistic correspondent —who advocates the great principle of "Divide the havings of the few among the wants of many "—who is so fluent upon tbe subject of the advantages that, might, could, would or should flow from the adoption of socialistic ideas if only the blind individualists could be brote2ht to see what an immense advantage it would he to—the Socialists! The three quarters of a column winch this apostle of "Divide yours for multiplication of mine," devotes to a high flight into the regime of socialistic imagination would, to use a local country saying "Charm a toad off a turf-stack," could the reader do, as the writer has very evidently done, shut his eyes very persistently to certain very awkward secialistically destructive facts. Chief among these is the fact—now well established— that Socialism can only exist as a parasite—a blood sucker—upon the individualistic body—politic. Among the many things which " Common Justice" says he has "proved "and "shown," I find no mention of the recent socialistic break-down—New Australia, the socialistic colony in Paraguayan Cha.to, Seuth America. Here Socialism has been tried on its merits, weighed and found wanting. This is one of the inconvenient facts ignored by your ecstasied cerrespondent as a mere detail ; he prefers very much to soar above such petty obstructions into the nebulous heaven of socialistic pos- sibilities. It is refreshing to see the sublime faith C. J. has in himself, his cause—and in Joshua ! Especially is this the case when we find one living man who will declare his belief that the walls of Jericho did fall before the potent impact or " noise," and so confidently ven- tures to prophesy the speedy advent of a like end to individualism by a like cause. Now, if the blowing of their own trunipata by Socialists, will do this, it is indeed "God help Individualism"! No need for trumpet drill here ; 'it seems to be one of the gar' of Socialists, and they are ever ready to "elevate their horn." It is a noble doctrine, that of the " have nots " to apportion among themselves the belongings of the " haves,":with the glorious prospect of a fresh apportionment when they had spent their share ! The walls of English inelividuaiism are much • weaker than I take them to be if they crumble before the " ramming "and blatant bellowings of social faddists, however those of Jericho may have fared. As the parasite cannot exist apart from its victim—or the graft away from its scion—it might be crud to request these gentry to go to this town of mural instab- ility and so make old England a place where Socialists cease from troubling, and Individualists are at rest. In other words, as these alienators apwar to have so mush faith in Jericho, how would it be if they went there and so" Leave.their country for their country's good ?" But alas ! the pleasing prospect cunjured up by this enchant- ing thought is speedily blighted by the remembrance that—where the individualistic hack is, there also will be the socialistic flea—for " greater things have lesser things, upon their backs to bite 'em," we English have the Socialists, " And so ad irtfinitum." Nor are these " fleas " always of the " industrious " type ; too often are they of the Micawber kind awaiting the providential " turning up " of other folk's property.-- Unsocially yours,
JOHN PEERS.

THE RECTOR AND THE DRINK TRAFFIC. Sir,—The Rev. F. W. Willis told his audience in the Council Chamber of the Town Hall on Wednesday last, that in his opinion, "the drink traffic, was not wrong," One is reminded or. reading this, of the sayingof " Sir Lucius O'Trigger," in speaking of the literary effort of Mrs. Malaprop " " She must be deeply read to write like that." So with our ( stimable friend the Rector, lie must be deeply read to speak like that. What, ! 'llse drink traffic not wrong, not evil? This is truly anaszing ! who, I ask having any pretence to comtrwn sense, and obser- vation, could in the face of tie coo mu i evidence sup- plied by the public presa and public opinimi, come to such a conclusion, except a clergyman whose interest lay in patren'zing the big guns of" the trade." The Rec- tor is usually unfortunate in his public utterances, and his obssrvations on lids subject no Wednesday last are no exc.ption to the rule. Of all sul jsees elssthe should have a7::.1,.d this. As a Christian Minister one would shotsis he; duty to at least aLets;its frsiii ee!egis'n3 "die tracie;" and that publicly. But the Rector is far f rem 'Aug " cut e" and he give 1 his in aeon fer not " going for " the traffic, be telling his 1 hearsts, that he was indebtsd to eiir Gilbert Greenall and Sir Apdrew Walker for help in the shape of deviations. Se that what he had appfarsd o centrovert he admitted. But the Rector was most unlortunate in his proposed remedies, for in trying " to be all things to all men," he pleases no one. First, does anyone in Warrington think for a moment, that if the Rector was asked to support an association for "the reduction of the number of pub- lic houses." (his own proposal) he would give it ? No, certainly not, the Rector would be conspicuous by his , absence from such an association. And why ? the reason is obvious. "because I am indebted to Sir Gilbert and Sir Andrew." The interests of " the trade," are diametrically opposed to the interests of true religion, of humanity, of happiness, not only of our peeple but of the little children, the poor tender little ones so dear to the heart of our good God. The Rector may fooltimself to the top of his bent by talking platitudes, and deceiving his own conscience on this vital question, but the truth is plain to any person of ordinary observation. The drink traffic is an evil, which is eating the vitals out of our people ;it is the most prolific source, of irreligion, immorality, vice, pauperism and lunacy, in existence. Desperate evils re- quire and call for desperate remedies. You will never crush out the terrible evils which are the outcome of this drink traffic, this cursed drink traffic, except by adapt- ing the real remedy, viz., total abstinence. Till the powers that be shall recognize this fact, till Christian ministers and those responsible for the education of our children—who will be the manhood of the future—are convinced of the necessity of forewarning them of the terrible evils of intemperance, and of enlisting them in the ranks of such estimable societies as the Good Terri- plass, the Rechabites, the Band of Hope, the League of the Cross, and kindred a.ssoc.iations,the evil of drink will continue on its course like a roaring lion, devouring all who come within reach of its claws. Ah but the pity of it, that those whose duty it is to place the interests of Jesus Christ, the interests of their flock, both spiritual and temporal, before every other consideration, should have "An itching palm," and forget the true interests of their people and their nation. I would Idre with every consideration for the position of the Rector to ask him to peruse and ponder over the following words of Henry Edward Cardinal Manning, ere he gives himself away finally to the enemy of grace and religion. His eminence wrote as follows :—" When I see around me every day the wreck of men, women, and children, from the highest to the lowest class, the utter desolation of homes once happy and innocent, the destruction of the domestic life of the millions of our great working class, upon whom the whole fabric of our common wealth must rest, I feel that temperance and total abstinence ought to be familiar thoughts in the mind even of those who have never in all their life been tempted to excess. If they would all conscientiously unite by example, by word, and by influence to save those who are perishing in the dangers from which they themselves are happily safe, many a ssul and many a home now fearfully wrecked, would, I believe, be saved." When St. Paul told the Christians in Rome that" it is good not to eat flesh and not to drink wine, nor anything whereby thy brother is offended, or scandalieed,or made weak," (Romans xiv. 21), he certainly did not intend to limit the wide reach of this principle of Christian charity to meats offered to idols. . . . If any self-denial on our part, in things that are lawful, and to us altogether safe, shall help, or encourage, or support, or given even a shadow of strength, to those to whom such lawful things are not only dangerous but often deadly, then assuredly the love of souls will prompt us to place our- selves at their side, and, in sharing their acts of self-denial, to give them a hand and a heart of sympathy. In conclusion let me say that if the temperance move- ment was taken up by the churches and the people saved from the ravages of this fearful evil of intemper- ance the donations of brewers would be as a drop in the ocean compared with the support of the people. If we could only win the Rector to the side of total abstinence which is the only real remedy, then truly we could say a him "Quantum mutatus ab illo !"—Yours, kc., J. C. DALTON. Vice-president of " The League of the Cross." Warrington, April 30th, 1894.

Sir,—While giving the Rector of Warrington credit for the utmost sincerity when addressing the annual meeting of the Police Court Mission on Wednesday,April 20th, use cannot but hone that your numerous readers will pause before they accept as sound and true the re- marks which he then made. The position which he holds as Rector entitles the com- munity to expect clear guidance, and the influence of a beneficent example, upon all questions affecting their religious, moral, and social well-being, and it is because in this instance his utterances are calculated to mislead, that the following observations are made. That the Rector took the highest ground by appealing to the Bible is matter for congratulation, for unless the temperance cause is fought out upon the principles contained in that book, it cannot succeed. From one occupying his posi- tion a correct interpretation of the Scripture i is natur- ally expected, and when emphatic statements are made fegarding the teaching they contain, it is not too much to expect that sufficient proof will he advanced in sup- port thereof. Two statements were made by the Rector concern- ing the tcac!iing of the Bible upon the drink question, Viz :- 1. That the Bible fram beginning to end allowed the moderate use of intoxicating drink. 2. That the Saviour gave it in large quantities,not for its medicinal qualities, but for onjoyment. As no evidence in support of these statements was adduced, it will he sufficient at present to deny the truth of both these pronositions,and to ask the Rector to bring forward proof sufficient to convince reasonable persons who are not prepared to accept bald or unsupported as- sertions simply because they are uttered by one occupy-

ing an influential position in the Church. If he fail publicly,to do this within a reasonable time,your readers may draw their own conclusions as to his ability to fur- nish proof, and possibly I may have something more to say upon the subject, for it can be clearly shown that in the Bible, Divine sanction is not given to the use of in- toxicating drink, and that it is morally certain, our Saviour neither made nor used wine that was intoxicat- ing.

The Rector states that assertions have been made re- garding the silence of the Cnureh people of Warrington upon the drink question. lam not aware that this charge has been advanced, but the silence of the clergy of the Established Church has been animadverted upon, and is not that very silence a most significant fact ? When men like the Bishop of London,theßishop of New- castle, the late Bishop Lightfoot, Archdeacon Farrar, Canon Wilberforce, Canon Barker, and a host of others have done,or are doing such splendid service in the tem- perance cause, why is it that one listens in vain for any manly, straightforward utterance by the clergy of this town on this most important subject? Why de not the clergy of Warrington follow the example of the clergy of other places, and take their stand side by side with tem- perance reformers of other denominations in united efforts to combat the great evil of intemperance, the results of which, all must admit, are of the most appal- ling description and call for combined action on the part of all who have at heart the welfare of our country. Int) the suggestions of tile Rector for remedying intem- perance, it is not necessary to enter further than to sug- gest that a perusal i4f the reports On intemperance,of the Convocations of Canterbury and York would greatly enlighten him as to the benefits of prohibition. The York report states that "the amount of intemperance . . . is always in proportion to the rate of wages and the amount of facilities provided for obtaining drink." "In the 1,273 parishes and districts of the Southern province (states the report of the Southern Convocation) where there are no houses for the sale of intoxicating drink, drunkenness,pauperism, s.nd crime are found to be very rare. In the large parishes of the north there are not so many districts without places for the sale of drink, yet in those which do exist, the same result of lessened drunkenness and crime is obtained."

It is to be hoped that when the Rector again speaks upon this subject, his remarks will be such as will net hinder but really help those who are fighting what the late Duke of Albany described as "The only terrible enemy England has to tear."—Yours truly, EDWARD T. REED. 17, Museum-st„ Warrington, May 2nd, 1894.

div.head: RUNCORN TECHNICAL INSTRUCTION INSTITUTE.
div.p: THE RUNCORN TECHNICAL INSTRUC- TION INSTITUTE.
NEW PROMISES OF SUPPORT.

A meeting of the General Committee of the Runcorn Technical Instruction Institute was held on .Nlenday evening in the Town Hall, Runcorn, for the purpose of deciding what course should be adopted to raise subscriptions on behalf of the Technicai Instruction Institute. Mr.F. Wiswall occupied the chair, and the other gentlemen present were the Revs. Canon Maitland Wood, and Dr. Gastaldi, Messrs. F. J. Norman, J.P., S. Taylor. J.P., W. Handley, W. Hankinson, A. R. Norman, R. Posnet, E. Key, Dudley, F. A. Lake, (law clerk), and %. Marshall, (secretary). In the course of his op,ming remarks, the chairman stated that donations already promised al-nounted £242 103. The new promises were :—Mr. Bowdes, architect for the institute, £lO 103.; Mr. Ro lands, £5.; Mr. T. Handley, £5; Mr. Bellamy, £5. Then there were the donations promised by Mr. Brunner, M.P., and other prominent townsmen, which had already been published. Ile considered their position to be a most hopeful one, and he was sure all present must feel extremely gratified with the proe'ress made towards realizing the amount required. The estimate for the work was £3,500, which sum would be increased to £.4,000 when the cost of equipping the schools was included. As before mentioned they had £lOOO from the Science and Art Department ; £440 from the Cheshire County Council; and £450 accumulated from the Id.rate. The first payment to the contractor of £350 had ben authorised and they would be expected to furnish another similar amount in a month's time. Therefore it was necessary that the sum promised should be sent in so that they might be ready to meet that demand.
_ Mr. F,J. Norn ; Has not Mr. Brunner promised £l,OOO
The Chairman : Yes. I have reason to believe that we shall get £l,OOO from Mr. Brunner pr,riding we raise a similar amount.

Mr. Taylor thought the people of Runcorn had already subscribed £450 through the id. rate, and thereforo by the subscription ne, another £5O they would be dble to claim the first £5OO from Mr. Brunner. The Chairman replied that this would be laid before Mr. Brunner %Ai° would not, he (the Chairman) was sure, be too exacting towards them. He could safely say that from a conversation which he had had with Mr. Brunner hirruielf upon the subject. Their business that evening was to appoint gentlemen who would undertake to collect funns.

Mr Taylor proposed that letters be sent to those gentlemen who had made promises asking them to kindly remit their amounts to the treasurer in order that the committee might be able, when the time arrivsd to pay the next instalment to the contractor.—Mr. Handley seconded the motion which was unananously carried.—ln accordance with the earnest request of several gentlemen present Messrs. E Key and Dudley undert.)ok to canvas am6ngst the Oddfellows of the town, for subscriptions, and Mr. Handley promised to do his utmost in the same direction amongst the trades unions. Dr. Gastaldi also signified his willingness to take a collecting book and work in his own parish. It was further resolved to approach the principal land- owners and traders in the district, and that this should be done by personal visits being made by various members of the committee and other gentlemen.— Being appealed to for assistance by those present, Mr. Posnett informed the Chairman that he could enter upon the books a promise on behalf of the Highfiehl Tannery Company of a donation of £2O. •(Hear, hear,) Shortly afterwards the chairman announced that Mr. A. R. Norman had just given him a promise of £lO towards the fund—(Hear, bear,)—and he was sure that all presetit were very thankful to both Mr. Posnett and Mr. Norman for their kindness and liberality. (Hear, hear.) No other business of public interest was transacted.

div.p: RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY. AUTHORITY.

Mr. John Mclntyre presiderl over the usual fort- nightly meeting of the above authority, held on Tuesday at the Workhouse, Dutton. The other gentlemen present were the Heys. J. lianby, and .1. W. N. Tanner, Messrs. J. Knowle, J. Williams, J. Weir, T. Lewis, C. IV. Davenport, E. Aaron. C. T. Whitley, W. Pickering, T. Baxter. C C., J. Stokes, J. Brandreth, E. Bratherton, J. Ashton, clerk ;G. div.head: APPOINTMENT OF MEDICAL OFFICER.
div.p: THE APPOINTMENT OF MEDICAL OFFICER.
The Clerk reported the receipt of a letter from the Local Government Board, sanctioNing the ra-appoint- ment of Dr. Adams, as medical officer for the ensuing year, at a salary of £l2O per annum.

div.head: SCARLATINA AT BUDSVOILTII.
div.p: SCARLATINA AT BUDSVOILTII.

A telegram was read by the Clerk from Dr. Adams, stating that he could not attend the meeting, and re- porting the existence of four cases of scarlatina in Bud- worth village. He had taken the usual precautionary measures to prevent the spread of the disease.
THE AUTHORITY AND THE SHIP CANAL BILL.

Mr. Brandreth stated that the solicitors of the Man- chester Ship Canal Company had sent a draft of the clause they proposed to insert in the above Bill for the purpose of protecting the Authority with regard to sewerage. That clause provided tt.at "nothing in the Act should prejudice, vary, or affect the rights, and remedies of the Runcorn Rural Sanitary Authority," Mr. Brandreth continuing said that the Committee who had the matter Ira hand had resolved that the Clerk be authorised to instruct their Parliamentary agents to watch the progress of the Bill and to see that the clause was inserted. He moved the confirmation of the Com- mittee's minutes.—Mr. Aaron seconded and the resolu- tion was carried.

div.head: INFECTIOUS DISEASES lOSPITAL AT MOORE.
div.p: THE INFECTIOUS DISEASES lOSPITAL AT MOORE.

Mr. Williams stated that the committee appointed to consider the purchase of the hospital at Moore had re- solved at their last meeting that the hospital be retained and that Messrs. Williams and Heywood, the Clerk, and the Medical Officer wait upon the officials to make the best terms; also to settle the form which the letter to Mr. Jackson should take with relerence to the hospital. He moved the adoption of the report.—Mr. Woodward seconded and it as agreed upon.
TILE PROPOSED SEWERAGE OF HELSBY TELEGRAPH WORKS.

The Clerk intimat9d that a letter had been received from the Telegraph Manufacturing Company. fielsby, saying that Mr. Farrington had called and they had agreed regarding the course and style of the drains, to be constructed across Mr. Adamson's field. The cost as shown would be £23 81. Si., including the cesspool on their land. The company also agreed to contribute 20 per cent, of the cost of construction providing the Sani- tary Authority, maintained it afterwards. The drains of two blocks of houses belonging to the company will be diverted into the cesspool, free of the ditch, thereby having the ditch free from pollution, arid this at the ex- pense of the company.—Mr. Brandreth proposed, and Mr. Woodward seconded that the matter be deferred un- til the appointment of a Parochial Committee under the Parish Councils.—Carried.

Ruans FOOTBALL.

" Tho third time and the last " is an old saying with more or less truth in it—probably less. Saturday was tlie third time Warrington encountered Sr. Helens Re- creation—and it is the last match of the season. A large gate assembled at this seini-performance, and the cul- mination of the season was all the more pleasant because it ended in a victory for the Wirepullers. The St. Helens men made themselves pretty certain of a victory because they brought their" champion" team, whereas War- rington lacked the:services of one or two of their best players such as Jolley, Nevins, and Carey. However, " blessed are they that expect little for they shall not be disappointed." St. Helens were completely dis- appointed for they were beaten by one goal and a try to nil.

Things have turned out curious in the Junior League Competition. The match between St. Mary's and Latch- ford on Monday night, at which each team were strug- gling to obtain possession of the 'cup presented by Mr. Percy Davies, will be remembered for a long time by those who witnessed it. In zeal and determination it was something like the struggles of the famous Kilkenny cats, but of course the players did not quite annihilate each other. Flow long they would have continued had not the darkness put an end to the combat it would be hard to say. The cup, the inh:ment cause of this terrific struggle, could not be presented to the winners for the simple reason that there were no winners to present it to, and Mr. Warren bad to carry it away again.

As for the game itself, the result is quite in keeping with the play. Although it was a very lucky try scored by Latchford, neither side Ind any decided advantage over the other. The Latchford men were by far the burlier of the two, and they adopted just the right tac- tics for their side in not allowing the ball to get loose more than they could help, for the St. Mary's team was the superi,r team in the loose. In the forward rank, Latchford were slightly superior, and Dakin especially distinguished himielf, and it was owing to his exertions that the try for Latchford was obtainei. In the half back department, there were four excellent players en- gaged, the most prominent being Bennett for Sc. Mary's and Houghton, for LAtchford. The Sc. Marc's three- quarter rank was superior to the Latchford quartette, but they did not get so very many opportunities of dis- tinguishing themselves, as they were looked after too wed by their opponents. Burton was the best of the lot, although his usual drop goal did not coins off this time. Lie had however very hard lines at times in not putting the finishing touch to pieces of excellent play. Raybold, Liampson, and Warburton also played v,ry welt. On the Latchford side, Smith and Lord were the shining 01 the full backs, Chapman of Latchford was the best. Roughley did some good work, but he was not very sure in his play, and almost let his opponents in several times.

The cup competition has opened the eyes of a good many people as to the quantity of good players which the Warrington .team can draw upon if necessary. Many ot the junior players are well worthy of "promotion," and the Rugbeists haw; no cause to fear the decay of their code for a long time to come in Warrington, for there is such au array of talent in till rising gr;neriaion as will continue to ke..p W.trringt.)a in the loYcfront in the foot- ball world.

div.head: GENERAL TALK.
div.p: A GENERAL TALK.
BY MR. H. WHITHAM.

I think it is quite possible that our friends will have no objection to allowing the question of So- cialism rest awhile. We, who recognise evolution as an all round fact may, in Fabian fashion, be con- tent to seize opportunity by the hand as we go along. Some time ago I read in an English paper of an incident that happened somewhere in Wales. At one of the churches, a tea party was being ar- ranged for, and the bidden guests were enjoined to bring along with them their own tea and eatables. I was amuse 4 at reading this, and the idea struck me that possibly the good folks at the head of that church had been in America taking lessons. By the way, I should Fay that all places of worship are in this hand of equality, called churches. Having no State Church,ail denominations are like the people, the rich and the poor and so forth, equal. Artemus Ward would have reminded his readers that a " goak " was around. I don't need to do this, as I am quite satisfied that my readers by this time fully understand how stupendous a "goak" it ie,this talk of American equality. I want to talk church, but first take the follow- ing as a sample of American liberty. " Cincinnati, Rev. C. I. Grandieon, D.D., president of Bennett Greensbero, N.C., is here as a delegate-at- large from North Carolina to the prohibition con- vention. He registered at the Gibson House and went into the dining room for breakfast, where the head waiter showed him to a seat. He ordered breakfast and was told all right. In about ten minutes the head waiter came to him and informed him that the proprietor desired him to eat in the ordinary or servants' dining room. This Grandison refused to do. At dinner time, when Grandison went into the diningroom,service was flatly refused. He immediately left the hotel declaring that he would bring suit for damages against the Gibson House Company." I think it quite likely that law will be on the side of the coloured man, but law is not all-powerful. In some districts the railway companies provide special cars for the coloured folks. I suppose the darky reminds the good white Christian too much of his sable majesty below, hence the repugnance to a too close ietimacy. A few days since, my wife received two admis- sion tickets to what was called the " Church Roll Call," one of the tickets was, of course, for the ad- mittance of my own poor self. While sitting listen- ing to the somewhat monotonous call of the roll, 1 could'nt help thinking that you in the 'oulti country did'nt know everything. Our first business was of course, eating. Everything on the tables had been provided by the members. The way this ía done differs very much from your way of giving trays, and is, I think much better. A very large com- mittee of ladies is appointed. These contrive to see the various lady, members and suggest what may be required. The result is well furnished tables, and no running about from table to table. Another example of this way of doing things may be given further on. When the eating and drinking are done with, all proceed to the church and get seated, the minister calls his deacons to the rostrum—we have no pulpits—me of whom reads out the Roll Call. Of course there is no need for this to be a solemn affair. A young and sprightly man will ask his audience, to stand up.quick and so out out" hear' as each one hears his or her name. A bit of amusement may be created, and enjoyed without it degenerating into anything unseemly. At the same time it enables each one to become ac- quainted with names they have not known. Some 465 names of members were gone through to the evident saftifaction of an present. Another very good plan adopted here is to give what are called "surprise parties." In all towns, and I suppose this occurs in all countries, the people generally divide themselves up into small and intimate circles. It is within the experience of every one to know that just a few within these circles become special favourites, and are looked upon as leaders The idea is to please these favor- ites of fortune, and a surprise party is arranged. It is decided to visit him some evening at his home. In the meantime each one of the visiting party pro- vides himself or herself with some toothsome mor- sel. On arrival the visitors take complete posses- sion, arid proceed to lay the table and have a high good time of it, the favourite entering into the fun with a sort of pardonable pride. Very often astill • greater surprise awaits him. Just recently a young lady friend of ours had a surprise party, and, 'kr hen the table was cleared away a nice gold watch made its sudden appearance, and was a pleasing surprise to the recipient. It is quite usual that, while the fun is going on, a cart draws up, and a nice desk or book case makes its appearance. Even without these more costly gifts, a surprise party is a very nice way of pleasing one who has friends all round. • Its cost is very little inasmuch as all join, and the debris can be made use of next day. Notwith- standing all the secrecy that is supposed to exist a slight, hint is generally conveyed so that the busi- ness may go along smoothly. During the winter months, the young folks con- trive to get a heap of enjoyment out of the long evenings. some time ago I, although not one of the , young tolke, was invited to attend a sheet and pillowslip party. The participants of such a party are made up of an equal number of the two sexes. Each one is provided with a sheet and pillowslip. ! The latter with two peep-holes for the eyes is pulled over the head and the sheet is wound around the body so as to completely hide the identity of the person. This done by the friends around, the males are taken behind a screen at one end of the room and the females similarly are placed at the other end. The M.O. standing in the middle of the room or hall, ald having all the names before him calls out to John Jones and al ary Smith to come forward. • This is done until all are mated, they then proceed to make.what was to m°, mess, surprising marching figures on the floor. I should -ay that each lady and gentleman give, privately a fictitious name to the M.C. so that t hey ,lo not know who their partners are and no telking neleweil. While they are walk- ing through all the figures, an oyster supper is being , provided in another rontn, to whichp when the signal es given, the gent lernan has the honour of escorting his partner. l'revious to the pillowelip being removed the gentleman is called upon to pay for two,then the slip slips off and he sees the pretty face he has had the pleasure of marching about. It is usual to finish up with dancing. There are hun- dreds of different ways of styling these gatherings. All that the management has to do is to single out some portion of the dress for carricature, the nalre grotesque it is made and the more fun. It would give lots of fun at a ball to see the most unmatch- able and loud colours adorning the necks of the merry makers. When the Americans go in for fun they certainly do " lick all creation." In the field sportingmen have what are known as "Gymkahana races." These generally round off the day's sports and afford no end of amusement, to the spectators. The contestants strip off their coats and waistcoats, and with saddle on the ground, at the word "go" saddle up and get into their °utter gar- ments with all possible speed, for the winner must arrive at the stake clothed and in his right 'mind. The egg and spoon race discounts a circus perform- ance. The winner must ride from start to finish with. a whole egg in a wooden spoon. There is no limit to the number of eggs that he may break, but the winning egg must have travelled the entire course. The riders in a cigar and umbrella race must smoke a mild Havana while carrying a raised umbrella. This race is a fine thing for the umbrella trade, as it is a very rare thing for even the winner to arrive at the post with his umbrella in a perfect condition. When reading of these little matters as happen- ing here in New England one can scarce help the memory reverting to the time when things were not quite so free and easy. Even now it is easy to see that there are two very distinct peoples shouldering each other day by day. The one always ready to stand by the old Blue Laws, and the other respecting neither law nor person and referring to the President of the U.S. as "the stuffed prophet of Bazzard's Bay." Connecti- cut is known as the "Land of steady habits." Its Blue Laws spread throughout New England at one time and remind one of Buckle's History. They are so called because they were printed on blue paper. The following are a good sample._
"No one sfi'all be a freeman or have a vote unless he is converted and a member of one ef the churches allowed in the dominion."

" No dissenter from the essential worship of this dominion slip be allowed to give a vote for elect- ing magistrates or any other officer." "No food or lodging shall be offered to a heretic." "No one shall croFs the river on the Sabbath but an authorized clergyman." "No one shall travel, cook victuals, made beds, sweep houses, cut hair or shave on the Sabbath day." "No one shall kiss his or her children on the Sab- bath or feasting day." "The Sabbath day shall begin at sunset Satur- day." "Whoever wear clothes trimmed with gold, silver or bone lace above one shilling a yard shall be pre-

" The wielder 3 of Vie Willow " commended to make their pleasant 11111 f if.; on th Arpley Cricket Ground, on Siturdav, when they opene.l the season with a contest with Olat;am. It was the first appearaticn of the latter club after an ab.=ence ext,.reling ov,r many years. Old- ham had tho advantage of going in first, and as the "sad" Was wet the visitors received much benefit. The whole of their wickets were dow.n for 85, while Warring- ton for live wickets aiumiul,tted the capital sum of 68. Of this J. J. Crosield scored 26, and Bates, the new pro- fessional , 19. The popular R. Smith, through some un- fortunate cause, failed to make anything more imposing titan a "duck's egg." This was quite a dispiriting per- formance from the dashing captain. But I don t suppose, it will happen often.

By the way, two new faces showed themselves on the sward in t.e Warrington ranks in the persons of P. Gallon, of Widnes, and J. Wordsworth, who was of some note as a Yorkshire cricketer. B )th are uputed to be capital additions to the club, and though only enjoyipg sh:)rt innings they proved themselves very cap tble players. I did not hear, by the way, until this week. that W.Podinore had resigned for the present season. It is owing, I understand, to the exigencies of business. I am sure the cricketing public will be as sorry to hear this as the club wore when Mr. Podmoro tendered his re- signation. We all know how prominent Mr. Podmore has been in the club as a batter and a fielder,for the last 18 years,a,ncl wo hope that lie will again re-appear among his comrades at least next season, if not this. Last year Mr. Podinore's total scores were nearly the highest in the club.

The public gave Bate the professional quite an ovation, which he thoroughly deserved. His batting was excel- lent, and was perhaps excelled by his bowling. Mr. Bate besides having been prominently connected with Yorkshire County has played in all England matches, and has been engaged as professional in two or three South African Clubs.

The Sankey Wesleyans gained a rather unexpected victory against the Penketh Friends on Saturday. After having ten " ducks " in their inAtch with the Y.INI.C.A. on the previous Saturday it was not expected that they would stand very much chance with such good bowling as the Penketh Friends possess. However, the unex- pected happened and the Wesleyans won by no less than 55 to 30. To this Peers in a large measure contributed, for although only scoring eight, he kept his wicket up for a long time, although there was a very bad light at the time. Bailey scored eleven, and J. Booth woo was the only one who did not make a "duck "the previous week, was again the top scorer with 15. Smith and Waring were the most destructive with the ball on the Friends side. When the Friends went in, they could make no headway whatever with the bowling of Watkins and Bailey, and not one gained double figures, the high- est scorer being Waring with seven. The game was only just won in time, by Sutton being smartly stumped by Jefferson.

The Sankey Wire Mills team made short work of the Penketh Weslevans. The Wesleyans went In first, but so deadly was the bowling of Simpson and Hobson that the whole team was out for the poor score of 14. Hob- son took two wickets for only one run, and Simpson six for six. Needless to say the wiremen quickly passed this score, accomplishing it without the loss of a wicket and then run uti a total of 76 for the loss of only seven wickets. F. Williams and A. Marshall were the top scorers with 21, and 19 respectively. The Wesleyans had evidently something to learn before they can hope to master their opponents of last Saturday. The second team of the Wire Mills also scored a victory at the ex- pense of Hough Greet' by 57 to 26,J. Evans with 23 runs to his credit made his colleagues look rather small ar- burton and Dutton were very distructive with the ball.

NOT.—We shall be glad to receive from secretaries of local cricket clubs a list of the scoring at the matches in which they take pvrt. Unless these are sent in not later than Wednesday morning, however, they will not be inserted.

div.head: BAKERS' AGITATION AT ST. HELENS.
div.p: BAKERS' AGITATION AT ST. HELENS.

The Amalgamated Unian of Corporative Bak-nts and Confectioners have just intimated to the masters of S. Helens that the following conditions of work and wages will come into operation on Monday next, and express a hope that they will be acceptable :-1. That work shall commence not earlier than 3 a.m. on Monday, and not earlier than 5 a.m. on Tuesday, Wednesday, Thurs- day, and Friday in each week, and at 12 midnight on Friday for Saturday's work. 2. That the minimum rate of wages be : For forehands, Ms. second hands, 235.; juveniles over eighteen years and under 21 years, 245. per week. Wages at present above the minimum not to he interfered with. The third, fourth, and fifth resolutions refer ta packs and smalls, the price to be 2s. per 100 loaves, including all sizes, and the 6th rule stipu- lates that public baking be abolished on Saturdays. In connection with the bakers' dispute at St. Helens, it is stated that the operative bakers and confectioners are discussing a project for the starting of a union bakery. It has been decided that in the event of the employers holding out against what the men consider their just and reasonable demands, the men them- selves should start and bake bread for the public. This union bakery is not intended to be in opposition to the tr,s de in general, but only to such employers as refuse to comply with the demands of the men. The dispute will be brought under the notice of the Trades Council, with the view of obtaining the support of other trades.

ANNUAL MEETING.

The yearly meeting of the members of the Run- corn Tonic Sol Fa Prize Ctloir was held on Monday evening, in the Ellesmere-street Schbolroom, Run- corn under the presidency of Mr.P. Speakman, J.P., C.C. There was a large attendance, The Chairman , in opening the proceedings congratulated them up- on the success that had attended their efforts luring the , past season. He was glad to be identified with that society. They all knew he was associated with a great many movements, recreative, philanthropic, and com- mercial, but although his time was greatly occupied, he knew the charms of music, and how that without it commercial pursuits were unendurable. (Applause.) Messrs. Burrows and Gandy submitted the report of the past season which showed a satisfactory increase in the membership, in the vice-presidents, and in the honorary members. From a musical point of view the season had been the most bri di ant (applause)—the choir had experi- enced. Mr.Newall,tre3.surer,reported that the season com- menced with an adverse balance, and that it closed with one of about £7. They were to be congratulated, how- ever, that the deficiency was sat larger considering the numerous expenses they had boen put to in the produc- tien of the oratorios given during the year. It was general.ly admited that the gain to the society in the matter of reputation was well worth the expenditure. The report and balance sheet were adopted on the pro- position of Mr. Holford. Votes of thanks to the officers for their services during the year were ac- corded, after which the election of aficials took place • with the fallowing result :—President : Mr. P. Speakman; vice-presidents: the same as the previous year ;' conductor : Mr. Holford ; treasurer : Mr. Newall ; secretary : Mr. Wesley Cook ; assistant secretary : Mr. E. Kniveten ; librarian: Mr. Wilsen Newall ; chairman of committee: Mr. Hugh Hughes ; committee : Mesdames Newall, Stubbs, Leath- wood, and W. Coventry, Misses Massey, K. Edwards, Smith, and Williams, Messrs. William Cooke, W. Coventry, A. Clare, John Leathwood, T. Burrows, S. Harrison, W. Pendlebury, .and C. Leathwood.- It was resolved that the choir take part in the Crystal Palace Festwal on the 14th July.

div.head: KICKING OUTRAGE AT ST. HELENS.
div.p: KICKING OUTRAGE AT ST. HELENS.
DYING DEPOSITIONS TAKEN.

A middle-aged widow, named Mrs. Carney, of Wright-street, Greenbank, St. Helens, was removed to the Providence Hospital in that town, on Sunday afternoon, suffering from terrible injuries alleged to have been inflicted by a man named Thomas M'Cue, a chemical labourer, who has been taken into custody on a charge of doing g,revious bodily harm to the woman. The allegation is that late on Saturday night M'Cue, who also resides in Wright-street, was quarrell- ing with another man, and Mrs. Carney asked them to desist. M'Cue then turned upon her, knocked her down and kicked her, inflicting aerious internal injuries, Dr. Jamieson (assistant to Dr. M'Nicoll.) Dr. Fred Knowles, and Dr. Potter (assistant to Dr. Knowles) were sum- moned. The woman was found thoroughly exhausted, and it was feared death would terminate her sufferings. The man M'Cue was apprehended. The condition of the injured woman grew still more serious on Sunday night, and it was deemed advisable by Chier-constable Wood that her despositions should be taken, to be produced as evidence in the event of her death. For this purpose the attendance of Alderman J. C. Gamble, a borough magistrate, was secured, and that gentleman, accompanied by Mr. B. Brewis, the assistant. Magistrate's Clerk, visited the Providence Hospital shortly before ten o'clock. Chief-constable Wood also attended, and the prisoaer, Thomas M'Cue, was present in custody. The woman was in an extremely weak con- dition, and was evidently suffering severe pain. From her statement, which was given on oath, it appeared that shortly before midnight on Saturday the woman's son and the prisoner M'Cue were quarrelling in the street near her house. She endeavoured to persuade her son to enter the house, and the prisoner then assaulted her.

div.head: ST. HELENS TOWN COUNCIL
div.p: ST. HELENS TOWN COUNCIL

The quarterly meeting of the St. Ilelens Town Council was held on Wednesday, the Mayor (Alder- man Sinclair) presiding. Alderman C. J. Bishop referred to the adoption of bye laws for lodging-houses, and said some of them seemed unreasonable. He thought the inspection proposed— viz., of 63. a week houses, where a lodger or two was taken—was a great interference. How many people in that chamber, he asked, had their ceilings whitened every year ?—Councillor Foote : None.—Another regu- lation was that the bedroom floors were to be washed ()free a week. Was that reasonable ? (" No.") The landlord was to cause every court or courtyard to have a hard pavement. That was not required ordinarily, where footpaths were laid. There 'NT/Jere many regul- tions with which he (Mr. Bishop) agreed, but he thought some consideration ought to be shown. Mr. flatton said he agree] with Alderman Bishop. Mr. John Forster (chairman of the Health Committee) said the byelaws were the model byelaws of the Local Government Board, and applied generally to houses where lodgers were taken all over the country. The only point left to the,r, as the local authority, was in fixing the rateable value and rental. In St. Helens it had been fixed ;it a:low figure,so as not to include any more houses than were really necessary. Houses would not come within the byelaws unless the landlords were called upon to be registered by the medical officer. At present any premises let for lodeings, but which did not come under the head of common lodging-houses, could do what they chose, and could overcrowd without the slightest con- trol.—The hyelaws were approved. Alderman Gamble, C. 8., chairman of the Watch Com- mittee, moved the confirmation of the minutes. There was a recommendation that the police force be increased by one inspector and five additional constables, and the chairman explained that when Sir Herbert Croft,lnspec- tor of Constabulary,inspected the force two months ago, he called their attention to the fact that although they had a constable to every LOGO inhabitants, which was considered sufficient for the town some years ago, their calculations must not only be based on popula- tion but upon the area of the borough. The additional cost would be about £4oo.—Councillor F. R. Dixon- Nuttall seconded the confirmation of the minutes, which was agreed to.

Mr. Martin, chairinhn of tho Park Committee, announced that Messrs. Doniton, the pottery manufac- turers, had sent in a design for a handsome fountain which they wished to present to the new Taylor Park. If the Council did not approve of the fountain, they would present £25 worth of vases. (Applause.)—lt was decided to approve of the gift of a fountain, and leave the arrangements in the hands of the committee.

The Manchester Ship Canal Bill was on Tuesday before the Select Committee of the House of Lords. It sought sanction for the construction of several jetties ; but the chief feature of the bill was a special clause under which the Company desired to be exempted from section 24 of the Railway and Canal Traffic Act, 1888: This section set forth that the Company must send to the Board of Trade a schedule of their tolls and charges for revision. It was contended by counsel that the sec- tion should not apply to the Ship Canal Company, inas- much as they were only just making a business, and sufficient experience had not yet been obtained with regard to the working of the tolls. The Committee ' decided that the special clause asked for by the promo- ' tors should stand part of the bill, but should not apply to any property of the Company except the actual Man- chester Ship Canal. Drawing 'attention to the wharfage ratespayable to the Mersey Docks Board, Mr. Balfour Browne cefiatended that as vessels proceeding directly• into the Ship Canal did not derive any advantage from the piers and wharves of the Mersey Docks Board, they should be freed from the obligation to pay wharfage rates upon goods which might be brought to Manchester by ship and afterwards returned to Liverpool. The existing impost militated, against ships coming up the canal. It was a great hindrance to trade,: and the Ship Canal Company asked to ,be relieved of it. The Com- mittee adjourned till to-day. The Manchester Ship Canal Bill was again before the Select Committee of the House of Lords • on Wednesday. The chief clause considered sought to exempt the canal docks and basins from the dues of the Mersey Docks board for local or partial traffic. Mr. Marshall Stevens was examined, and said the Company did not object to pay dues on cargo passirpg over the Mersey Docks, but they thought it unfair that Portions of cargo pissing along the Mersey directly to the port of Manchester and then being returned to Liverpool ehoulkbe liable to wharfage charges. After discussion, and with the sanc- tion of he Committee, the wharfage clause was adopted, to the effect that no vessel loading or discharging in the port of Manchester any part of its cargo which should be ' landed on any of the piers of the Mersey docks should be liable to pay wharfage charges, but all vessels taking any such cargo from the port of Manchester to the piers belonging to the Mersey Docks Board er taking cargo therefrom te vessels in the port of Manchester should be aubject to pay the Doak:: Board tonnage rates. MILLOWNERS AND THEIR WATER SUPPLY.

div.head: IMPORTANT LITIGATION.
div.p: IMPORTANT LITIGATION.

The Appeal Court,consisting of Lords Justices Lindley, Lopes, and Kay, had before them last Thursday the ea-4e of Fairclough and Sons, of Warrington, v. the Manchester Ship Canal Company. This was an appeal of tire defend- ants from/an order of Justice Kekewicti, who refused their application to vary a consent order restraining the witlicirawal by them of water from the river Mersey,con- trary to the Act., and interference with the navigation. The appeal should have Come before the court on a pre- vious occasion, but,owing to the indisposition of Lord Justice Kay, it had been postponed until he was able to attend, Sir Richard Webster saying that the case was of tich great importance to the Canal Company that it was desirable to have it tried by three appeal judges. Sir Richard Webster, Q.C., Mr. Fletcher Moulton, Q C., and Mr. Sebastian appeared for the appellants, and Mr. Fin- lay, Q.C., Mr. Warmington, Q.C.', and Mr. Hughes re- presented the respondent. A plan of the canal was pro- duced in court.

Mr. Moulton said the order appealed from was an in- terlocutory one made upon a motion. He called their lordships' attention to Manchester, Eccles, and Bowdon. The canal cut in very Many places the tortuous old course of the rivers Mersey and Irwell, and for a ncrtain length of the canal the Irwell had been extirpated, so that now the Ship Canal was what was the Irwell. Latchford Locks were the last; of Plie locks on the canal. There were tidal openings at the estuary, but so far as the land was concerned these locks might be taken as the last. At Howley Weir there were the Mersey Mills. When the powers were obtained for making the canal these millowners opposed the bill on the ground that if the water of the Irwell and Mersey were taken away by the canal and passed down the bed of the cabal they would lose their water rights, and in consequence a cer- tain clause was put in for their protectioe. Alter bear- ing further argument. Lord Justice Lindley did not think that any injury could be done by the appeal on the motion standing over till the trial of the action, seeing that the operation of the injunction was suspended till the 31st of May, and the trial could be expedited so as to come on at the com- mencement of next sitting. Upon those terms this appeal was ordered to stand over till after the trial, the costs being made costs in the action.
THE QUEEN'S VISIT TO MANCHESTER: FINAL

div.head: ARRANGEMENTS.
div.p: ARRANGEMENTS.

The precise route to be followed by the Queen when she comes to Manchester to open the Ship Canal on the 21st inst. has now been definitely settled. Her Majesty will'arrive at London Road Station about 4.30 p.m.,and will be received there by the Lord Mayor of Manchester. A carriage will be in waiting to convey Her Majesty to the Town Hall via Piccadilly, Market-street, and Cross- street, where an address will be presented by the Cor- poration while Her Majesty remains in the carriage. The Queen will then proceed by way of Mount-street, Oxford-street. All Saints', Stretford Road, and Chester Road to Trafford Wharf, on the Stretford side of the canal, near Trafford Road swing bridge, where she will be received by the Lord Lieutenant and the Chairman and Directorss of the Ship Canal Company. Her Majesty will then embark on the Almiralty yacht Enchantress, which will steam round the docks and down the canal nearly as far as Mode Wheel locks escorted by gun- boats of the Royal Navy and other vessels, returning to Trafford Wharf. There she will re-enter the carriage, and proceed by way of Trafford Road, Regent Road, Egerton-street, Chester R0a.,1,, Deansgate, St. Ann-street, St. Ann's Square, Exchange-siTeet, and Victoria-street to Exchange Station, where the Roy:. I train will be in waiting to convey Her Majesty to Scotland. Addresses will be presented to the Queen by the Directors of the Ship Canal Company on board the Enchantress, and by the Corporation of Salford within the borough. The following out of this programme will probably involve a stay of something like three nours. Shareholders in the Ship Canal Company will, it is understood, have accommodation provided for them on Trafford Wharf, and the public will have access to the Salford quays. The military arrangements will be under the control of the General Commanding the District.

div.head: WANDEPING LUNATIC.
div.p: A WANDEPING LUNATIC.

CZ'An elderly man named William Malone was charged at St. Helens on Tuesday with being .a wandering lunatic, he having been found in Park-road on Monday night by Police-constable Lewis. Dr. Casey said the man had dangerous delusions. He said he had electricity all over, and that people whispered in his ears, and told him to commit suicide. He was likely to commit suicide unless taken care of. An order for his removal to Rainhill Asylum was made. SERIOUS ACCIDENT TO A Sr. HELENS FARMER.

Henry Parr, a middle-aged farmer, living on Sutton- road, between Rainhill and St. Helens, was coming along Peasley Cross-lane, St. Helens, on Saturday afternoon, when his pony got restive at a steam tramcar which was approaching. Parr got out to take hold of the animal's head, but he was knocked down and run over. The trap was then upset. Parr was taken to the hospital, where Dr. Bellew found he had sustained a compound fracture of the thigh and left arm, and was bruised all over :he body.

div.head: HAYDOCK.
div.p: HAYDOCK.

NSW BOWLING GREEN AT HATDOCE.—On Saturday afternoon, Mr. T. D. Grimke-Drayton, J.P., managing director of Messrs. Richard Evans and Co. ,opened a new bowling green in Haydock,. where a most flaurishing bowling club is in existence. The bowling green is ax extension of the old ground, and altogether the two • greens have an area of about 100 square yards. Mr. John Jackson gave a history of the scheme, stating that . the total cost of the green had been £l2B, the men had done £5O worth of work, and now they were about LEO in debt. Mr. Drayton then sent the first ball across the,% green. and heartily congratuleed the members, saying when Haydock men did work, it was work well done. . He declared the gree.n open, and hoped Haydock people '- would have many a grand day's bowling upon it.—Mr: Edwin Jackson proposed a vote of thanks to Mr. Draf ton, and hoped that was only the start of a gigantie • recreation society in Haydeck.—Mr. Johnsen seconded,, and the resolution was carried.—Mr. Drayton returned thanks, and with Mr. Barrett played the first game ite the new green. BAYDOCE LOCAL BOARD.—At a meeting of the Haydoek- Local Board on Thursday, Mr. T. D. kirimke-Draytnn was re-appointed chairman, and Mr. Batharry vice- chairman.—lt was decided to present a memorial to the County Council, praying that the township be divided in- to three wards, and that the number of members be in- - - creased from nine to twelve. The memorial stated that the township Was formed in 1873, with an area of 2,480 acres. The district since that year had increased very largely, and the growth had been continuous. A com- munication was read from Superintendent Brassington. intimating that it was proposed to appoint an additional , constable for Haydock, in consequence of tn• growing population and crime being ou the increase. The Chairman said he would like a return as to the crime in the township. The whole of the cases from Haydock went to Newton, and his opinion was that it was the other way. The qu,-2stion wa3 postooned for a month.—Dr. Hayward was re-appoirawl discriet medi- cal officer.

At the Liverpool kssizes on Thursday a young domes- tic servant named blargaret O'Toole, residing at West Kirby. obtained £l5O •lamages against James H. Parkin- son, dentist. Liverpool, on account of an assistant hav- ing placed the girl undn. chloroform and extracted all her t?eth without having obtained permission to do so. IMPERIAL IA RLIAMENT.

THURSDAY. In the House of Commons on. Thursday evening Mr. WOODALL, in reply t a question, said the forty-Aight hours week arrangement at Woolwich Arsenal was work- ing very smoothly and to the general satisfaction. Sir U. Kay-S'nuttleworth informed Mr. Vincent that about sixty life-saving boats for the torpedo-boat destroy- ers had been ordered from Germany by contractors for the latter boats, but said that if larger orders became desirable the Admiralty would: as usual, endeavour to arrange for the manufacture in this country. It was, however, the clear duty of the Admiralty to endeavour to obtain the best articles and inventions for war, whe- ther Foreign or British. The House resumed the debate on the motion for the second reading of the Registration Bill, to which an. amendment had been moved lay Sir E. Clarke declining to proceed with the bill in the absence of proposals for the redress of the inequalities in the distribution of elec- toral power. The debate was continued until midnight, and then adjourned until Friday.
